units.title: Greetings & Everyday Phrases
units.description: First words in French — Core greetings and polite phrases.

questions.prompt: How do you say "hello (informal)" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Salut" is the casual hello you use with friends and family; "Bonjour" is the polite one.

questions.prompt: How do you say "hello (formal)" in French?
questions.explanation: "Bonjour" is the polite hello you use with strangers, in shops or at work; "Salut" is only for friends.

questions.prompt: How do you say "good evening" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Bonsoir" is the greeting for the evening. "Bonjour" is used during the day.

questions.prompt: How do you say "goodbye" in French?
questions.explanation: "Au revoir" is the standard way to say goodbye in any situation; "Bonjour" is hello, not goodbye.

questions.prompt: How do you say "see you soon" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "À bientôt" means "see you soon": "bientôt" means "soon", and you say it when you expect to meet again before long.

questions.prompt: How do you say "please" in French?
questions.explanation: "S'il vous plaît" is the polite way to say please; with a friend you say "s'il te plaît".

questions.prompt: How do you say "thank you" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Merci" is the standard way to say "thank you" in French, and it works with anyone.

questions.prompt: How do you say "you're welcome" in French?
questions.explanation: "De rien" literally means "it's nothing" and is the everyday reply when someone says "merci".

questions.prompt: How do you say "excuse me" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Excusez-moi" is the polite "excuse me" for getting a stranger's attention. It uses the vous form.

questions.prompt: How do you say "sorry" in French?
questions.explanation: "Désolé" means "sorry" and is used to apologise. A woman writes it "Désolée".

questions.prompt: How do you say "yes" in French?
questions.explanation: "Oui" is the French word for "yes". The other options are greetings or welcomes, not answers to a question.

questions.prompt: How do you say "no" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Non" is the French word for "no", the opposite of "oui".

questions.prompt: How do you say "how are you?" in French?
questions.explanation: "Comment allez-vous ?" is the polite way to ask how someone is; "Comment vous appelez-vous ?" asks their name instead.

questions.prompt: How do you say "I'm fine, thanks" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Je vais bien, merci" literally means "I am going well, thanks". French uses the verb aller (to go) to say how you are.

questions.prompt: How do you say "what is your name?" in French?
questions.explanation: "Comment vous appelez-vous ?" is the polite way to ask someone's name (literally "how do you call yourself?"); "Je m'appelle..." is the reply.

questions.prompt: How do you say "my name is..." in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Je m'appelle..." means "my name is..." (literally "I call myself"); you follow it with your name.

questions.prompt: How do you say "nice to meet you" in French?
questions.explanation: "Enchanté" is what you say when you meet someone for the first time; a woman writes "Enchantée", which sounds the same.

questions.prompt: How do you say "good night" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Bonne nuit" is said at bedtime or late at night when parting; "Au revoir" is just a general goodbye.

questions.prompt: How do you say "see you tomorrow" in French?
questions.explanation: "À demain" means "see you tomorrow" because "demain" means "tomorrow".

questions.prompt: How do you say "welcome" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Bienvenue" is what you say to greet someone arriving, like "welcome" in English.

questions.prompt: How do you say "of course" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Bien sûr" means "of course"; you use it to say yes or to agree warmly.

questions.prompt: How do you say "I don't understand" in French?
questions.explanation: "Je ne comprends pas" is the negative of "je comprends" (I understand): French wraps the verb in ne ... pas to say "not".

questions.prompt: How do you say "can you repeat, please?" in French? ___
bank: Parlez plus lentement, s'il vous plaît
questions.explanation: "Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?" politely asks someone to say something again: "répéter" means "to repeat" and "pouvez-vous" means "can you".

questions.prompt: How do you say "do you speak English?" in French?
questions.explanation: "Parlez-vous anglais ?" is a polite question made by putting the verb before "vous"; "anglais" means "English".

questions.prompt: How do you say "good luck" in French? ___
questions.explanation: "Bonne chance" means "good luck"; "chance" is feminine, so the adjective is "bonne", not "bon".

units.title: Numbers 1–100
units.description: Counting in French — Cardinal numbers from one to a hundred.

questions.explanation: "un" is the French number 1; it is also the word for "a" before a masculine noun, as in un café.
"deux" is the French word for 2; the final x is silent when the word stands alone.
"trois" is the French word for 3; the final s is silent, so it sounds like "trwah".
"quatre" is the French word for 4; it starts with qu-, which sounds like a k.
"cinq" is the French word for 5; note the unusual -nq spelling at the end.
"six" is the French word for 6; it looks like the English word, but on its own it is pronounced "seess", with a clear s sound at the end.
"sept" is the French word for 7; the p is silent, so it sounds like "set".
"huit" is the French word for 8; the h is silent and it sounds like "weet".
"neuf" means nine (9); don't mix it up with "cinq" (5) or "treize" (13).
"dix" means ten (10); it is the base for 17, 18 and 19 ("dix-sept", "dix-huit", "dix-neuf").
"onze" means eleven (11); it is the first of the special words for 11 to 16, so it is not built from "dix".
"douze" means twelve (12); it comes right after "onze" (11).
"treize" means thirteen (13); like the other numbers from 11 to 16, it ends in -ze.
"quatorze" means fourteen (14); it comes from "quatre" (4), like fourteen comes from four.
"quinze" means fifteen (15); "quatorze" is 14, so don't mix them up.
"seize" means sixteen (16); it is the last special word before French counts "dix-sept" (ten-seven).
"dix-sept" means seventeen: ten ("dix") plus seven ("sept"), joined with a hyphen.
"dix-huit" means eighteen: ten ("dix") plus eight ("huit"), joined with a hyphen.
"dix-neuf" is built as dix (ten) + neuf (nine), joined with a hyphen, just like "dix-huit" (eighteen).
"vingt" means twenty. Its final -gt is silent, so it sounds like "vin".
"vingt et un" means twenty-one; 21, 31, 41 and so on use "et" (and), unlike "vingt-deux" (22).
"trente" means thirty (30); it is the tens word that comes after "vingt" (20).
"quarante" means forty; don't mix it up with "quatre" (four) or "cent" (one hundred).
"cinquante" means fifty; it starts like "cinq" (five), just as fifty starts like five.

questions.prompt: The French word for "one hundred" is…
questions.explanation: "cent" means one hundred; French just says "cent", not "un cent".

units.title: Family & People
units.description: Talking about people you know — Family members and everyday words for people.

questions.explanation: "la mère" means mother; "la" shows it is a feminine noun, unlike "le fils" (son) or "le voisin" (neighbour).
"le père" means father; its partner word is "la mère" (mother).
"la sœur" means sister. It is feminine, so it takes "la", and it is spelled with the joined letters œ.
"le frère" means brother, a male sibling; don't confuse it with "la sœur" (sister) or "le cousin" (cousin).
"le fils" means son; the final s is pronounced ("feess"). "l'enfant" means any child, not specifically a son.
"la fille" means daughter (it also means girl). "le fils" is the son and "la sœur" is the sister.
"la grand-mère" means grandmother: grand + mère (mother), joined with a hyphen.
"le grand-père" means grandfather: grand + père (father). "la grand-mère" is the grandmother.
"la tante" means aunt, the sister of your mother or father.
"l'oncle" means uncle. The word is masculine (un oncle), and le becomes l' before the vowel.
"le cousin" is a male cousin; the masculine form ends in -in, pronounced nasally.
"la cousine" is a female cousin: add -e to le cousin and pronounce the n. "le cousin" is the male form.
"le mari" means husband. For wife, French usually says la femme.
"l'épouse" means wife; in everyday speech French more often says "ma femme" (my wife).
"l'ami" is a male friend; a female friend is "l'amie", with an extra -e.
"l'amie" is a female friend; the extra -e marks the feminine (a male friend is "l'ami").
"l'homme" means man; the h is silent, so le becomes l'.
"la femme" means woman (and also wife); it is pronounced "fam".
"l'enfant" means child, a boy or a girl; le or la becomes l' before the vowel.
"le bébé" means "baby". The noun is masculine, so it takes "le" even when the baby is a girl.
"le garçon" means "boy". Its counterpart for a girl is "la fille".
"le voisin" means "neighbour", the person who lives next door. A female neighbour is "la voisine".
"le collègue" means "colleague", someone you work with. Note the accent on the first e, and that a woman is "la collègue".
"le professeur" means "teacher", especially in secondary school. In everyday speech people often shorten it to "le prof".
"l'étudiant" means a (male) student; a female student is "l'étudiante".

units.title: Colours & Clothes
units.description: Describing what people wear — Common colours and clothing items.

questions.explanation: "rouge" means "red". It already ends in -e, so it stays the same for masculine and feminine nouns.
"bleu" means blue; "gris", "vert" and "violet" mean grey, green and purple.
"vert" means green; "noir", "rouge" and "rose" mean black, red and pink.
"jaune" means yellow; "rouge", "noir" and "marron" mean red, black and brown.
"noir" means black; "violet" is purple, "bleu" is blue and "gris" is grey.
"blanc" means white; "noir" is black, "bleu" is blue and "rose" is pink.
"gris" means grey; "marron" is brown, "jaune" is yellow and "rouge" is red.
"marron" means brown, and it never changes its ending (des chaussures marron); "gris" is grey, "vert" is green and "blanc" is white.
"rose" means pink; "bleu" is blue, "noir" is black and "violet" is purple.
"violet" means purple; "rouge" is red, "jaune" is yellow and "marron" is brown.
"la chemise" means a shirt; "la robe" is a dress, "les gants" are gloves and "la veste" is a jacket.
t-shirt → le t-shirt. Common colours and clothing items.
"le pantalon" means trousers, and it is singular in French although "trousers" is plural in English; "la jupe" is a skirt, "le pull" a sweater and "la chemise" a shirt.
"la robe" means a dress; "les bottes" are boots, "le manteau" is a coat and "la jupe" is a skirt.
"la jupe" means a skirt; "les bottes" are boots, "le manteau" is a coat and "les chaussettes" are socks.
"les chaussures" means shoes; "la veste" is a jacket, "les gants" are gloves and "le pantalon" is trousers.
A jacket is "la veste"; it is feminine, so it takes "la". Don't confuse it with "le manteau", which is a longer, warmer coat.
A coat is "le manteau"; it is masculine, so it takes "le". A lighter jacket would be "la veste".
A hat is "le chapeau"; it is masculine, and its plural adds -x: "les chapeaux".
A scarf is "l'écharpe"; the word is feminine, but "la" shortens to "l'" before the vowel "é".
Socks are "les chaussettes"; don't confuse them with "les chaussures", which are shoes.
A sweater is "le pull", short for "le pull-over"; it is masculine, so it takes "le".
A belt is "la ceinture"; it is feminine, so it takes "la".
Gloves are "les gants"; they come in pairs, so the word is plural with "les" (one glove is "un gant").
Boots are "les bottes"; the word is plural, so it takes "les" (one boot is "une botte").

units.title: Days, Months & Seasons
units.description: Talking about time and calendar — Days of the week, months, and seasons.

lessons.title: Days, Months & Seasons 1
lessons.subtitle: Talking about time and the calendar

questions.explanation: "lundi" means "Monday", the first day of the French week. Days of the week take no capital letter in French.
"mardi" means "Tuesday", the day after "lundi". It is written with a small letter in French.
"mercredi" means "Wednesday", the middle of the week. It is written with a small letter in French.
"jeudi" means "Thursday", the day after "mercredi". It is written with a small letter in French.
Friday is "vendredi", the day after "jeudi" (Thursday). French day names are written in lowercase.

lessons.title: Days, Months & Seasons 2
lessons.subtitle: Talking about time and the calendar

questions.explanation: Saturday is "samedi"; don't confuse it with "dimanche", which is Sunday, the day after.
Sunday is "dimanche"; it is the only day of the week that does not end in -di.
"janvier" means January. Unlike in English, French month names start with a lowercase letter.
"février" means February. Note the accent on the first e (é) and the lowercase f.
"mars" means March. It looks like the English word, but it is not capitalised and the final s is pronounced.

lessons.title: Days, Months & Seasons 3
lessons.subtitle: Talking about time and the calendar

questions.explanation: "avril" means April. It is close to the English word, with a v instead of the p, and it is written in lowercase.
"mai" means May. It sounds much like the English word and, like all French months, it is written in lowercase.
"juin" means June. Don't confuse it with "juillet" (July), which is the longer word.
"juillet" means July. The double l and the -et ending set it apart from "juin" (June).
"août" means August. Remember the circumflex on the u; the word is pronounced like "oo" or "oot".

lessons.title: Days, Months & Seasons 4
lessons.subtitle: Talking about time and the calendar

questions.explanation: "septembre" means September. It is like the English word, but it ends in -bre and is written in lowercase.
"octobre" means "October". Like all French months, it is written with a small letter.
"novembre" means "November", the month after "octobre". French months are written with a small letter.
December is "décembre". In French, month names take no capital letter, and note the accent on the é.
Spring is "le printemps". It is the only season that keeps "le", because it starts with a consonant; you say "au printemps" for "in spring".

lessons.title: Days, Months & Seasons 5
lessons.subtitle: Talking about time and the calendar

questions.explanation: Summer is "l'été". "Le" shortens to "l'" before a vowel, and "in summer" is "en été".
Autumn is "l'automne". The "m" is silent, so it sounds like "o-tonn", and "in autumn" is "en automne".
Winter is "l'hiver". The h is silent, so "le" shortens to "l'", and "in winter" is "en hiver".
Today is "aujourd'hui". Don't confuse it with "maintenant" (now) or "ce soir" (tonight).
Tomorrow is "demain". Its opposite is "hier" (yesterday).

units.title: Body Parts
units.description: Talking about the human body — Common parts of the body.

questions.explanation: Head is "la tête". It is feminine, so it takes "la", and the ê has a circumflex.
Hair on your head is "les cheveux". It is plural in French, unlike English; "un cheveu" is a single hair.
Eye is "l'œil". Its plural is completely different: "les yeux" (eyes).
"les yeux" means eyes. It is the irregular plural of "l'œil" (eye).
"l'oreille" means ear. It is a feminine noun, and le/la becomes l' before a vowel sound.
"le nez" means nose. It is masculine, and the final z is silent.
"la bouche" means "mouth". It is a feminine noun, so it takes la, as in « Ouvre la bouche » (Open your mouth).
"la dent" means "tooth". It is feminine, and the plural is les dents, as in « se brosser les dents » (to brush your teeth).
"le cou" means "neck". It is masculine, so it takes le; don't confuse it with le coude (elbow).
"l'épaule" means "shoulder". It is feminine (une épaule), and la becomes l' before the vowel sound é.
"le bras" means "arm". It is masculine, the final s is silent, and the plural is the same: les bras.
"la main" means "hand". It is feminine even though it ends in a consonant, so it takes la.
"le doigt" means "finger". It is masculine, and the g and t are silent, so it sounds like "dwa".
"la poitrine" means "chest". It is a feminine noun, so it takes la.
"le dos" means "back" (the body part). It is masculine, and the final s is silent.
"le ventre" means "stomach" or "belly", as in « J'ai mal au ventre » (I have a stomach ache). It is masculine, so it takes le.
"la jambe" means "leg". It is feminine, so it takes la; don't confuse it with le pied (foot).
Knee is "le genou". It is masculine, and its plural ends in x: "les genoux".
Foot is "le pied". The d is silent, and "on foot" is "à pied".
"Skin" is "la peau", a feminine noun. Don't confuse it with "la poitrine", which means chest.
"Face" is "le visage". It is masculine even though it ends in -e.
"Heart" is "le cœur", a masculine noun spelled with the joined letters œ.
"Elbow" is "le coude". "Le bras" is the whole arm, not the joint in the middle.
"Wrist" is "le poignet", a masculine noun. The final t is silent.
"Chin" is "le menton". "Le nez" is the nose, just above it.

units.title: House & Rooms
units.description: Talking about where you live — Rooms and household vocabulary.

questions.explanation: "House" is "la maison", a feminine noun, so you say une maison.
"Apartment" is "l'appartement". The article becomes l' before a vowel. The word is masculine (un appartement) and is spelled with a double p.
"la cuisine" means "kitchen", the room where you cook. It is feminine, and the same word also means cooking or cuisine.
"la chambre" is the room where you sleep, so it means "bedroom". Don't confuse it with "la salle à manger", the dining room.
"la salle de bain" literally means "room of bath", the room where you wash, so it is the "bathroom".

questions.prompt: The French word for "living room" is…
questions.explanation: "le salon" is the room where you sit, relax and welcome guests, so it means "living room".

questions.prompt: The French word for "dining room" is… ___
questions.explanation: "la salle à manger" literally means "room for eating" (manger = to eat), so it is the "dining room".
"le jardin" is the outdoor area with grass, flowers or vegetables next to a house, so it means "garden".
"la porte" is what you open and close to go into a room or a house, so it means "door".
"la fenêtre" is the glass opening in a wall that lets light in, so it means "window".
"le mur" is each vertical side of a room or building, so it means "wall".
"le sol" is the surface you walk on inside a room, so it means "floor". "le toit" is the roof and "le tapis" is a rug.
"le plafond" is the top surface of a room, above your head, so it means "ceiling".
"l'escalier" is the set of steps leading to another floor; French uses the singular where English says "stairs".
"Roof" is "le toit", a masculine noun. The final t is silent.
"Garage" is "le garage", a masculine noun. Careful: "la gare" means train station.
"Table" is "la table", a feminine noun. "Le tableau" looks similar but means a painting or a board.
"Chair" is "la chaise", a feminine noun. Don't mix it up with "la porte", the door.
"le lit" means bed, the piece of furniture you sleep in. Lit is masculine, so it takes "le". Don't confuse it with la chambre, the bedroom.
"le canapé" means sofa (couch). Canapé is masculine, so it takes "le".
"la lampe" means lamp, and it looks almost like the English word. Lampe is feminine, so it takes "la".
"le miroir" means mirror, the glass you look at yourself in. Miroir is masculine, so it takes "le".
"la clé" means key, the thing that opens a door. Clé is feminine, so it takes "la".
"l'étagère" means shelf. Étagère is a feminine noun starting with a vowel, so la becomes l'.
"le tapis" is the piece of fabric laid on the floor, so it means "carpet" or rug. "le sol" is the floor itself.

units.title: Common Verbs (infinitives)
units.description: Everyday actions — High-frequency verbs in their infinitive form.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to eat" is…
questions.explanation: "manger" means to eat. It is a regular -er verb, as in Je mange une pomme.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to drink" is… ___
questions.explanation: "boire" means "to drink", as in "boire de l'eau" (to drink water). It is an irregular verb, so learn it by heart.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to speak" is…
questions.explanation: "parler" means "to speak", as in "parler français". It is a regular -er verb.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to listen" is… ___
questions.explanation: "écouter" means "to listen", as in "écouter de la musique". Don't confuse it with "regarder", which means "to watch".

questions.prompt: The French word for "to read" is…
questions.explanation: "lire" means "to read", as in "lire un livre". "Regarder" means "to watch", not "to read".

questions.prompt: The French word for "to write" is… ___
questions.explanation: "écrire" means "to write", as in "écrire une lettre". Don't mix it up with "lire", which means "to read".

questions.prompt: The French word for "to sleep" is…
questions.explanation: "dormir" means "to sleep", as in "dormir huit heures". It is an irregular -ir verb.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to work" is… ___
questions.explanation: "travailler" means "to work", as in "travailler au bureau". It is a regular -er verb.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to study" is…
questions.explanation: "étudier" means "to study", as in "étudier le français". It looks like the English word "study".

questions.prompt: The French word for "to play" is… ___
questions.explanation: "jouer" means "to play", as in "jouer au football". It is a regular -er verb.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to walk" is… ___
questions.explanation: "marcher" means "to walk", as in "marcher dans le parc". It is a regular -er verb.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to run" is…
questions.explanation: "courir" means "to run", as in "courir dans le parc". It is an irregular -ir verb.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to swim" is… ___
questions.explanation: "nager" means "to swim", as in "nager à la piscine". It is a regular -er verb.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to cook" is…
questions.explanation: "cuisiner" means "to cook" (to prepare food); "jouer" is to play, "parler" to speak and "fermer" to close.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to buy" is… ___
questions.explanation: "acheter" means to buy, as in acheter du pain (to buy bread).

questions.prompt: The French word for "to sell" is…
questions.explanation: "vendre" means to sell, the opposite of acheter (to buy). Don't confuse it with attendre, which means to wait.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to open" is… ___
questions.explanation: "ouvrir" means to open, as in ouvrir la porte (to open the door).

questions.prompt: The French word for "to close" is…
questions.explanation: "fermer" means to close, the opposite of ouvrir (to open), as in fermer la fenêtre.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to look" is… ___
questions.explanation: "regarder" means to look (at) or to watch, as in regarder la télé. It takes no word for at.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to wait" is…
questions.explanation: "attendre" means "to wait" (for example, attendre le bus); "vendre" only looks similar and means to sell.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to help" is…
questions.explanation: "aider" means "to help"; it is a regular -er verb, as in « Je peux t'aider ? ».

questions.prompt: The French word for "to love" is… ___
questions.explanation: "aimer" means "to love", and also "to like" for things, as in « J'aime le chocolat ».

questions.prompt: The French word for "to want" is…
questions.explanation: "vouloir" means "to want" (je veux un café); "avoir besoin de" is different and means to need.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to need" is… ___
questions.explanation: "avoir besoin de" means "to need" (j'ai besoin d'aide); "avoir envie de" means to feel like, "avoir peur de" to be afraid of and "avoir faim" to be hungry.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to live" is…
questions.explanation: "vivre" means "to live" (to be alive, or to live somewhere), as in « Je vis à Paris ».

units.title: Animals
units.description: Common animals — Everyday animals, pets and wildlife.

questions.explanation: "le chien" means "dog"; it is masculine, so it takes "le".
"le chat" means "cat"; it is masculine, and the final -t is silent.
"l'oiseau" means "bird"; "le" becomes "l'" before a vowel, and the word is masculine.
"le cheval" means "horse"; it is masculine, and the plural is irregular: "les chevaux".
"la vache" means "cow"; it is feminine, so it takes "la".
"le cochon" means "pig"; it is masculine, so it takes "le".
"le mouton" means "sheep"; it is masculine, so it takes "le".
"la poule" is the live hen (feminine); chicken as meat is "le poulet".
"le canard" means "duck"; it is masculine, and the final -d is silent.
A rabbit is "le lapin" in French. Lapin is a masculine noun, so it takes le; le renard is a fox.
A mouse is "la souris" in French. Souris is a feminine noun, so it takes la, unlike most animals in this list.
A fish is "le poisson" in French. Poisson is masculine and is spelled with a double s, which gives the s sound.
A lion is "le lion" in French. The spelling is the same as in English, but the word is masculine and ends in a nasal vowel: the n is not pronounced as a separate sound.
A tiger is "le tigre" in French. Note the -re ending, where English has -er, and the masculine article le.
A bear is "l'ours" in French. Ours starts with a vowel, so le shortens to l'.
An elephant is "l'éléphant" in French. Éléphant starts with a vowel, so le shortens to l'. Note the two accents.
A monkey is "le singe" in French. Singe is a masculine noun, so it takes le.
A wolf is "le loup" in French. The final p is silent, and l'ours is a bear.
A fox is "le renard" in French. Renard is a masculine noun, and its final d is silent.
A frog is "la grenouille" in French. Grenouille is a feminine noun, so it takes la, and le canard is a duck.
A snake is "le serpent" in French. Serpent is a masculine noun, and its final t is silent.
"Turtle" is "la tortue". It is a feminine noun, so it takes "la" (une tortue).
"Bee" is "l'abeille". It is feminine (une abeille), and "la" shortens to "l'" before the vowel.
"Butterfly" is "le papillon". It is a masculine noun, so it takes "le" (un papillon).
"Spider" is "l'araignée". It is feminine (une araignée), and "la" becomes "l'" before the vowel.

units.title: Professions & Jobs
units.description: Talking about work — Common jobs and professions.

questions.explanation: "Doctor" is "le médecin", the usual word for the profession. You say "docteur" mainly when you address a doctor directly.
"Nurse" is "l'infirmier" for a man and "l'infirmière" for a woman. "Le" becomes "l'" before the vowel.
"Teacher" as a profession is "le professeur", used for secondary school and university teachers. In casual speech people often shorten it to "le prof".
"Engineer" is "l'ingénieur". It is masculine, and "le" becomes "l'" before the vowel.
"Lawyer" is "l'avocat". Watch out: the same word also means "avocado".

questions.prompt: The French word for "police officer" is…
questions.explanation: "Police officer" is "le policier". A female officer is "la policière".
"Firefighter" is "le pompier". It comes from "pompe" (pump), and firefighters work in "la caserne des pompiers" (the fire station).

questions.prompt: The French word for "cook" (the job) is…
questions.explanation: "le cuisinier" is the person who cooks as a job (a woman is la cuisinière); it comes from the verb cuisiner, to cook.
"Waiter" is "le serveur", from the verb "servir" (to serve). A waitress is "la serveuse".
"l'agriculteur" is the person who works the land and raises crops or animals; the article elides to l' because the noun starts with a vowel.
"le chauffeur" is a driver as a job, such as a taxi or bus driver (un chauffeur de taxi).
"le pilote" is the person who flies a plane; the word looks almost the same as the English "pilot".
artist → l'artiste. Common jobs and professions.
"le musicien" means "musician", a person who plays music; a woman is la musicienne.
"l'écrivain" means "writer", a person who writes books; "le" becomes "l'" before the vowel "é".
"le scientifique" means "scientist"; the word is the same for a man or a woman (la scientifique).
"le dentiste" means "dentist", the person who looks after your teeth (les dents); a woman is la dentiste.
"le comptable" is the person who keeps a company's accounts (un compte = an account); a woman is "la comptable".
"l'électricien" means electrician; "le" becomes "l'" because the word starts with a vowel.
"le plombier" is the person who fixes pipes and taps; it comes from "plomb" (lead), the metal old pipes were made of.
"le coiffeur" is the person who cuts your hair (la coiffure = hairstyle); a woman is "la coiffeuse".
"le journaliste" means journalist; the word is the same for a woman, only the article changes: "la journaliste".
"l'architecte" means architect; "le" becomes "l'" before a vowel, and the word is the same for a man or a woman.
"le soldat" is a member of the army; it is a masculine noun and looks close to the English word soldier.
"le secrétaire" means secretary; for a woman you say "la secrétaire", and the spelling stays the same.

units.title: Question Words
units.description: Asking questions in French — Core question words and phrases.

questions.explanation: "qui" asks about a person (who); quel asks which, and quand asks when.
"quoi" means what at the end of a question or after a preposition, as in "Tu fais quoi ?" or "De quoi tu parles ?"; at the start of a question French uses "que" or "qu'est-ce que".
"où" asks about a place (where); the grave accent separates it from ou, which means or.
"quand" asks about time (when); où asks where, and combien asks how much or how many.
"pourquoi" asks for a reason (why); the answer often starts with parce que (because).
"comment" asks about manner (how), as in Comment tu t'appelles ?; est-ce que only turns a sentence into a yes/no question.

questions.prompt: The French word for "how much" is…
questions.explanation: "combien" asks about a quantity or price, as in "C'est combien ?" (How much is it?); "quel" means which or what.

questions.prompt: The French word for "how many" is… ___
questions.explanation: "combien de" asks how many and is followed by a noun with no article, as in « Combien de frères as-tu ? ».
"quel" means which and agrees with its noun: quel livre, quelle heure, quels livres, quelles villes.
To ask whose something is, French says "à qui" (literally "to whom"), as in "À qui est ce livre ?" (Whose book is this?).
"qu'est-ce qui" is used when what is the subject of the verb, as in "Qu'est-ce qui se passe ?"; "qu'est-ce que" is used for the object.
"qu'est-ce que" is used when what is the object of the verb, as in "Qu'est-ce que tu veux ?"; "qu'est-ce qui" is used for the subject.

questions.prompt: The French word for "is it that…?" is… ___
questions.explanation: Put "est-ce que" in front of a statement to turn it into a yes/no question: Est-ce que tu viens ? (Are you coming?).

questions.prompt: The French word for "how old" is…
questions.explanation: To ask someone's age, French uses "quel âge" with the verb avoir: Quel âge as-tu ? (How old are you?).

questions.prompt: The French word for "what time" is… ___
questions.explanation: "quelle heure" asks about the time: Quelle heure est-il ? (What time is it?) or À quelle heure ... ? (At what time ...?).

questions.prompt: The French phrase for "who is it" is…
questions.explanation: "qui est-ce" is qui (who) plus est-ce (is it) and asks who a person is, as in Qui est-ce ? C'est ma sœur.

questions.prompt: The French phrase for "what is it" is… ___
questions.explanation: "qu'est-ce que c'est" asks what a thing is, as in Qu'est-ce que c'est ? C'est un livre; qu'est-ce qui alone is not a complete question.

questions.prompt: The French word for "where is" is…
questions.explanation: "où est" asks where one thing or person is (Où est la gare ?); for several things you use où sont.

questions.prompt: The French word for "where are" is… ___
questions.explanation: "où sont" asks where several things or people are (Où sont les clés ?); for one thing you use où est.

questions.prompt: The French phrase for "how are you (informal)" is…
questions.explanation: "comment vas-tu" uses tu, the form you use with a friend or family member; with a stranger you would say comment allez-vous.

questions.prompt: The French phrase for "what's your name (informal)" is…
questions.explanation: "comment tu t'appelles" literally means how do you call yourself and uses tu, so it is the informal way to ask someone's name.

questions.prompt: The French word for "which one" is… ___
questions.explanation: "lequel" means "which one" for a masculine noun (Lequel préfères-tu ?); it changes to laquelle, lesquels or lesquelles to match the noun.

questions.prompt: The French word for "which ones" is…
questions.explanation: "which ones" is plural, so you need the plural "lesquels" (Lesquels préfères-tu ?); lequel means only "which one".

questions.prompt: The French word for "why not" is… ___
questions.explanation: "pourquoi pas" means "why not" and is often used to accept a suggestion: On va au cinéma ? Pourquoi pas !

questions.prompt: The French word for "how far" is…
questions.explanation: "à quelle distance" asks how far away something is: À quelle distance est la plage ? (How far is the beach?).

units.title: Prepositions of Place
units.description: Describing where things are — Common prepositions used to locate things.

questions.explanation: "dans" means "in" when something is inside something else: dans la maison (in the house).
"sur" means "on" when something rests on top of something else: sur la table (on the table).
"sous" means "under", for something below something else: sous le lit (under the bed).

questions.prompt: The French word for "in front of" is…
questions.explanation: "devant" means "in front of", as in "devant la porte". Don't confuse it with "derrière" (behind).
behind → derrière. Common prepositions used to locate things.

questions.prompt: The French word for "next to" is…
questions.explanation: next to → à côté de. Common prepositions used to locate things.
between → entre. Common prepositions used to locate things.
above → au-dessus de. Common prepositions used to locate things.
below → en dessous de. Common prepositions used to locate things.
near → près de. Common prepositions used to locate things.

questions.prompt: The French word for "far from" is…
questions.explanation: far from → loin de. Common prepositions used to locate things.
inside → à l'intérieur de. Common prepositions used to locate things.
outside → à l'extérieur de. Common prepositions used to locate things.
opposite → en face de. Common prepositions used to locate things.
"autour de" means "around" in the sense of surrounding something, as in autour de la table (around the table). "vers" means towards.
against → contre. Common prepositions used to locate things.
"à travers" means "through", going from one side to the other, as in à travers la forêt (through the forest).
"le long de" means "along", following the length of something, as in le long de la rivière (along the river). "de" becomes "du" before a masculine noun: le long du mur.
"among" is "parmi", used for one thing in a group of several: "parmi les livres" (among the books).
"vers" means "towards", showing direction, as in Il marche vers la gare (He walks towards the station).

questions.prompt: The French word for "at (someone's place)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "chez" means at someone's place and goes before a person or pronoun: "chez moi", "chez Marie".
"de" means "from", as in Je viens de Paris (I come from Paris). It combines with le and les: du, des.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to (a place)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "à" is the basic way to say you go to a place: "Je vais à Paris."
"ici" means "here", as in Je suis ici (I am here). It is an adverb of place, not a preposition, so no "de" follows it.
"là" means there, the opposite of "ici" (here): "Le chat est là."

units.title: Telling Time
units.description: Talking about the clock — Time expressions and everyday time vocabulary.

questions.prompt: The French for "it's one o'clock" is…
choices: il est une heure et demie
questions.explanation: "il est une heure" uses singular "une heure" because it is one o'clock; other hours take "heures".

questions.prompt: The French for "it's two o'clock" is… ___
questions.explanation: "il est deux heures" means "it's two o'clock". French uses il est plus the number and heures, which is plural from two onwards.
"il est midi" means it's noon (12 p.m.); "minuit" is midnight.
"il est minuit" means it's midnight (12 a.m.); "midi" is noon.

questions.prompt: The French for "half past two" is…
questions.explanation: "deux heures et demie" means "half past two". French adds et demie (and a half) after the hour.

questions.prompt: The French for "quarter past three" is… ___
questions.explanation: "trois heures et quart" adds "et quart" (a quarter past) to three o'clock; "et demie" would be half past.

questions.prompt: The French for "quarter to four" is…
questions.explanation: "quatre heures moins le quart" means "quarter to four": French takes the next hour and subtracts a quarter. Trois heures et quart is quarter past three.
After a clock time, "du matin" marks the morning (a.m.): "huit heures du matin".

questions.prompt: After a clock time, "in the afternoon" (as in 3 p.m.) is…
questions.explanation: After a clock time, "de l'après-midi" marks the afternoon: "trois heures de l'après-midi" is 3 p.m.
After a clock time, "du soir" marks the evening (p.m.): "huit heures du soir" is 8 p.m.
"la nuit" on its own means at night, with no preposition needed: "Je dors la nuit."

questions.prompt: The French for "what time is it?" is…
questions.explanation: "quelle heure est-il ?" is how you ask "what time is it?". The verb and subject swap places (est-il) to form the question.
"une heure" means "an hour". Heure is feminine, so it takes une.
"une minute" means "a minute". Minute is feminine in French, so it takes une.
"une seconde" is a second, the smallest unit of time here; "une minute" is sixty of them.
"tôt" means early (Je me lève tôt), while "bientôt" means soon.
"tard" means late, the opposite of tôt (early): Je me couche tard.
"maintenant" means now, at this moment; "toujours" means always.
"bientôt" means soon, as in À bientôt! (See you soon!).
"plus tard" means later (literally 'more late'), as in À plus tard!
"toujours" means "always", something that happens every time. "rarement" means rarely, "tard" means late and "bientôt" means soon.
"jamais" means "never", not even once. "souvent" means often, "tôt" means early and "plus tard" means later.
"parfois" means "sometimes", now and then. "jamais" means never, "bientôt" means soon and "tôt" means early.
"souvent" means "often", many times but not every time. "toujours" means always, "rarement" means rarely and "maintenant" means now.
"rarement" means "rarely", almost never. "souvent" means often, "toujours" means always and "maintenant" means now.

units.title: Shopping & Money
units.description: Buying things in French — Everyday shopping and money vocabulary.

questions.explanation: "l'argent" is the general word for "money". "la pièce" is a single coin, and "les soldes" are the sales.
"le prix" means "price", what something costs. "le magasin" is the shop, "le portefeuille" is the wallet and "les soldes" are the sales.
"cher" means "expensive", costing a lot of money. Its opposite in this list is "gratuit", which means free.
"bon marché" means "cheap", and it never changes form: une robe bon marché. "gratuit" means free, and "cher" means expensive.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to pay" is… ___
questions.explanation: "payer" means "to pay", to hand over money. "acheter" means to buy, "vendre" means to sell and "coûter" means to cost.
"l'argent liquide" means "cash": notes and coins, not a card. "la monnaie" is the change you get back, or small coins.

questions.prompt: The French word for "credit card" is… ___
questions.explanation: "la carte de crédit" means "credit card", word for word a card of credit. "l'argent" is money and "la pièce" is a coin.
"le reçu" is the slip of paper you get after paying; "les soldes" are sales, "le portefeuille" is a wallet and "la monnaie" is change.
"le magasin" is the place where you go to buy things; the other words mean a banknote, a credit card and a price.
"le supermarché" is the big shop that sells food and household goods; "le client" is the customer and "le caissier" is the cashier.
"le marché" is the place with stalls where people buy fresh food; "les soldes" are sales and "le reçu" is a receipt.
"le caissier" is the person who takes your payment at the till; "le magasin" is the shop and "la pièce" is a coin.
"la réduction" is the amount taken off a price; "le prix" is the price itself and "le reçu" is the receipt.
"les soldes" is the period when shops cut their prices, and in this sense it is always plural in French.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to buy (shopping)" is…
questions.explanation: "acheter" means to get something by paying for it; "vendre" is to sell, "payer" is to pay and "coûter" is to cost.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to sell (shopping)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "vendre" means to give goods in exchange for money, the opposite of "acheter" (to buy).
"le client" is the person who buys in a shop; "le caissier" is the person who takes the money.
"le sac" is what you carry your shopping in; the other words mean a banknote, a price and a credit card.
"le portefeuille" is the small case where you keep your money and cards; "le sac" is a bag and "la pièce" is a coin.
"la pièce" is a coin, while le billet is a paper banknote.
"le billet" is a banknote, while la monnaie means change or small coins.

questions.prompt: The French word for "free (no cost)" is…
questions.explanation: "gratuit" means free of charge, while bon marché only means cheap.

questions.prompt: The French for "how much does it cost?" is… ___
questions.explanation: You ask the price with "combien ça coûte ?": combien means 'how much' and coûter means 'to cost'.

questions.prompt: The French word for "change (money back)" is…
questions.explanation: The coins and notes the cashier gives back are "la monnaie": "Voici votre monnaie." It is not 'money' in general, which is l'argent.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to cost" is… ___
questions.explanation: "coûter" means 'to cost', as in "Ça coûte cinq euros"; acheter is 'to buy', payer is 'to pay' and vendre is 'to sell'.

units.title: At the Restaurant
units.description: Ordering food in French — Restaurant vocabulary and useful phrases.

questions.prompt: The French word for "set menu (fixed-price meal)" is…
questions.explanation: "le menu" is a fixed-price meal with set courses; the list of all the dishes is called la carte.

questions.prompt: The French word for "waiter (in a restaurant)" is… ___
questions.explanation: The man who takes your order and brings your food is "le serveur"; a waitress is la serveuse.
"la serveuse" is a waitress, the feminine of le serveur (waiter).
"la table" is spelled like the English word but is feminine, as in "une table pour deux".
"la réservation" is a booking, as in "J'ai une réservation"; note that it is feminine and takes an accent on the é.
"l'entrée" is the starter in a French meal, not the main course; the main course is le plat principal.

questions.prompt: The French word for "main course" is…
questions.explanation: "le plat principal" is the main dish, served after the starter (l'entrée) and before the dessert.
"le dessert" is the sweet course at the end of the meal; the word is masculine in French.

questions.prompt: The French word for "the bill" is…
questions.explanation: In a restaurant you ask for "l'addition" at the end of the meal: "L'addition, s'il vous plaît."
"le pourboire" is the extra money you leave for the waiter, literally 'for drinking'.
"la fourchette" is the fork you eat with; le verre is a glass and le menu is a set meal.
"le couteau" is the knife you cut with; la réservation is a booking, le pourboire a tip and la serviette a napkin.
"la cuillère" is the spoon, a feminine noun; le verre is a glass, l'addition the bill and la table the table.
"l'assiette" is the plate you eat from; la becomes l' before a vowel. La serviette is a napkin, not a plate.
"le verre" is the glass you drink from; la fourchette is a fork and l'entrée is a starter.
At the table, "la serviette" is the napkin (it can also mean a towel); le serveur is the waiter.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to order" is… ___
questions.explanation: "commander" means to order food or drink; payer is to pay, réserver is to book and goûter is to taste.
"délicieux" means delicious, very tasty; salé is salty, froid is cold and sucré is sweet.

questions.prompt: The French word for "I'm hungry" is… ___
questions.explanation: "j'ai faim" means I'm hungry; French says literally 'I have hunger', using avoir, not être.

questions.prompt: The French word for "I'm thirsty" is…
questions.explanation: "j'ai soif" means I'm thirsty (literally 'I have thirst'); don't confuse it with j'ai faim, I'm hungry.

questions.prompt: The French word for "the check please" is…
choices: une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît
questions.explanation: "l'addition, s'il vous plaît" is how you ask for the bill (the check) at the end of a meal; la carte is the menu.

questions.prompt: The French word for "a table for two" is… ___
questions.explanation: "une table pour deux" is what you ask for at a restaurant when there are two of you; pour deux means 'for two'.

questions.prompt: The French word for "enjoy your meal" is…
questions.explanation: "bon appétit" is what you say to wish someone an enjoyable meal, just before they start eating.
"végétarien" means 'vegetarian' and is the masculine form; a woman adds -ne: "Je suis végétarienne."
"l'allergie" means 'allergy'; it is a feminine noun, and "la" becomes "l'" before a vowel.

units.title: Classroom Objects
units.description: At school — Everyday classroom objects and school words.

questions.explanation: "le livre" is a book you read; don't confuse it with "la carte", which means a map or a card.
"le stylo" is a pen for writing in ink; a pencil is "le crayon" and a notebook is "le cahier".
"le crayon" is a pencil, not a pen ("le stylo"); "la gomme" is the eraser you use with it.
"le cahier" is a notebook or exercise book you write in; a printed book you read is "le livre".
"la gomme" is an eraser and is feminine; don't confuse it with "la règle", which is a ruler.
"la règle" is a ruler for drawing lines; the same word also means a rule.
A desk is "le bureau", a masculine noun (un bureau). The same word also means "office".
A chair is "la chaise", a feminine noun (une chaise), used for any chair, not just in the classroom.
The classroom board is "le tableau", a masculine noun. The teacher writes au tableau (on the board).
"la craie" is the French for chalk, the stick you write with on a blackboard; it is feminine, so it takes "la".

questions.prompt: The French word for "bag" (like the one you take to school) is…
questions.explanation: "le sac" means 'bag', for example the bag you carry to school; a traditional school satchel is "le cartable".
Paper is "le papier", a masculine noun. A single sheet is une feuille de papier.
Scissors is "les ciseaux". Like the English word, it is always plural in French: des ciseaux.
Glue is "la colle", a feminine noun. It comes from the verb coller (to stick).
A calculator is "la calculatrice", a feminine noun related to calculer (to calculate).
A dictionary is "le dictionnaire", a masculine noun. Note the double n in the French spelling.
"la carte" means 'map' in the classroom; the same word also means 'card', or 'menu' in a restaurant.
A clock is "l'horloge". The article elides before the silent h, and the noun is feminine (une horloge).
A classroom is "la salle de classe", literally "room of class". It is feminine because salle is feminine.
homework → les devoirs. Everyday classroom and school vocabulary.
exam → l'examen. Everyday classroom and school vocabulary.
"la question" is spelled like the English word but is feminine, so it takes "la"; the answer you give is "la réponse".
"la réponse" means "answer", the reply to une question. It is feminine, so it takes la.
"la leçon" means "lesson". Note the cedilla on the ç, which gives it an s sound, and that the word is feminine.

questions.prompt: The French word for "timetable" (school schedule) is… ___
questions.explanation: "l'emploi du temps" is your school timetable, the schedule of your lessons for the week.

units.title: Technology & Devices
units.description: Everyday tech — Common devices and technology words.

questions.explanation: "l'ordinateur" means "computer". It is masculine (un ordinateur), and le becomes l' before the vowel.
"le téléphone" means "phone". It is masculine and spelled with ph and two é accents.
French borrows the English word: "le smartphone" is masculine; in everyday speech people also say "le portable".
"l'écran" is the screen of a phone, TV or computer; it takes l' because écran starts with a vowel.
A keyboard is "le clavier". The word is masculine, so it takes "le".
"la souris" means both the animal and the computer mouse. It is feminine, so it takes "la".
internet → internet. Common technology and device vocabulary.
"le courriel" is the official French word for an email. In everyday speech in France people also often say "le mail" or "l'e-mail".
"le mot de passe" is literally "the word for passing", which is a password. It is masculine because "mot" is masculine.
An app is "l'application", often shortened to "l'appli". It is feminine, and "la" becomes "l'" before the vowel.
A website is "le site web", often just "le site". "site" is masculine, so it takes "le".
"l'appareil photo" is literally a "photo device", which is a camera. "appareil" is masculine and starts with a vowel, so it takes "l'".
The battery in a phone or laptop is "la batterie". It is feminine, so it takes "la".
"le chargeur" comes from the verb "charger" (to charge) and is the device that charges your phone. It is masculine.
"les écouteurs" comes from "écouter" (to listen) and means headphones or earbuds. It is usually plural, so it takes "les".
"l'imprimante" comes from "imprimer" (to print) and means the printer. It is feminine, and "la" becomes "l'" before the vowel.
"la tablette" is a tablet computer, like an iPad; the noun is feminine, so it takes "la".
"la télévision" is the television; "l'écran" is only the screen, and "la tablette" is a tablet.

questions.prompt: The French word for "remote control" is… ___
questions.explanation: "la télécommande" is the remote control you use to change TV channels from a distance; the noun is feminine.
French uses the English word, and it is masculine, so it is "le wifi".
"le message" is a note you send to someone, for example by text; it looks like the English word, but remember it is masculine, so it takes "le".

questions.prompt: The French word for "phone call" is… ___
questions.explanation: "l'appel" means a phone call; "le" becomes "l'" because "appel" starts with a vowel.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to download" is…
questions.explanation: "télécharger" means to download a file or an app onto your device; "enregistrer" means to save.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to send" is… ___
questions.explanation: "envoyer" means to send, for example a message or an email; "recevoir" is the opposite, to receive.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to save (a file)" is…
questions.explanation: "enregistrer" means to save a file so you keep it; "télécharger" means to download.

units.title: Hobbies & Free Time
units.description: Talking about what you like doing — Common hobbies and leisure vocabulary.

lessons.title: Hobbies & Free Time 1
lessons.subtitle: Talking about what you like doing

questions.prompt: The French word for "to read (for pleasure)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "lire" means to read, for example books or comics in your free time.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to draw" is…
questions.explanation: "dessiner" means to draw with a pencil or pen; "peindre" is used for painting.

units.title: Feelings & Emotions
units.description: Describing how you feel — Common feelings and emotions.

questions.explanation: Happy is "heureux", as in Je suis heureux. A woman says heureuse.
"triste" means "sad"; "déçu" means disappointed, "surpris" surprised and "amoureux" in love.
"en colère" means "angry"; it is a fixed phrase that stays the same for masculine and feminine (il est en colère, elle est en colère).
"fatigué" means "tired" (je suis fatigué); a woman adds -e: "fatiguée".
"enthousiaste" is the safe way to say you are excited or enthusiastic about something; avoid "excité", which can sound sexual.
"effrayé" means afraid or frightened; in everyday speech French also says "j'ai peur" (I'm afraid).
Surprised is "surpris", which looks like the English word. A woman says surprise.
bored → ennuyé. Common feelings and emotions.
Nervous is "nerveux": English -ous often becomes -eux in French. A woman says nerveuse.
"calme" means "calm" and looks almost like the English word; it is the same for men and women.
"inquiet" means "worried" (the feminine is "inquiète"); "effrayé" means frightened, which is stronger.
Proud is "fier", as in Je suis fier de toi. A woman says fière.
Jealous is "jaloux", as in Il est jaloux. A woman says jalouse.
Confused is "confus" here, but careful: Je suis confus often means 'I'm embarrassed or sorry'. To say you don't understand, French speakers usually say Je suis perdu.
"gêné" means embarrassed or ill at ease; the other words mean grateful, comfortable and calm.
Relaxed is "détendu", from se détendre, 'to relax'. A woman says détendue.
Disappointed is "déçu", from décevoir, 'to disappoint'. Triste only means 'sad'.
grateful → reconnaissant. Common feelings and emotions.
"seul" means alone; to say you feel lonely, French says "je me sens seul".
confident → confiant. Common feelings and emotions.
curious → curieux. Common feelings and emotions.
"frustré" means "frustrated" and looks like the English word; "en colère" means angry.
hopeful → plein d'espoir. Common feelings and emotions.

questions.prompt: The French word for "in love" is… ___
questions.explanation: in love → amoureux. Common feelings and emotions.
"à l'aise" means comfortable or at ease as a feeling (je suis à l'aise); a comfortable chair is "confortable".

units.title: Transportation
units.description: Getting around — Transport and travel vocabulary.

questions.explanation: car → la voiture. Transport and travel vocabulary.
"le bus" is the bus; it is masculine, so it takes "le", while "la voiture" is a car and "le quai" a platform.
"le train" is the same word as in English and is masculine; the other options mean airport, car park and motorbike.
"l'avion" means "plane"; "le" becomes "l'" because "avion" starts with a vowel.
"le vélo" is the everyday French word for "bicycle"; "la voiture" is a car and "le bateau" is a boat.
"la moto" (short for "la motocyclette") means "motorcycle"; "le vélo" is a bicycle and "le camion" is a truck.
"le bateau" means "boat"; the other options are a bicycle, a truck and a driver.
"le taxi" means "taxi", the same word as in English, and it is masculine; "la voiture" is any car.
"le métro" is the French word for the "subway" (underground railway); the other options are a passenger, a ticket and traffic.
"le tramway" means "tram", and people often shorten it to "le tram"; "le bus" is a bus.
"le camion" means "truck", a vehicle for carrying goods; "le bus" carries passengers and "le bateau" is a boat.
"le billet" is the "ticket" you buy for a train, bus or plane; the other options are traffic, a train and a taxi.
"la gare" means "station", especially a train station; "la route" is a road and "le bus" is a bus.
"l'aéroport" means "airport"; "le" becomes "l'" because "aéroport" starts with a vowel.
"le quai" is the "platform" where you wait for a train or tram at the station; "la route" is a road.

questions.prompt: The French word for "driver (of a vehicle)" is…
questions.explanation: "le conducteur" is the person who drives a vehicle; la voiture, la moto and le camion are vehicles, not people.
"le passager" is a person who travels in a vehicle without driving it; the other words are a vehicle (le vélo, le tramway) and a platform (le quai).

questions.prompt: The French word for "to drive" is…
questions.explanation: "conduire" means to drive a car or other vehicle; voyager means to travel, arriver to arrive and voler to fly.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to fly" is… ___
questions.explanation: "voler" means to fly (it can also mean to steal); atterrir means to land, freiner to brake and conduire to drive.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to travel (on a trip)" is…
questions.explanation: "voyager" means to travel or go on a trip; conduire is to drive, voler to fly and arriver to arrive.
"la route" is the road that cars drive on; it is a feminine noun, so it takes la.
"la circulation" means traffic, the flow of cars on the roads, as in « Il y a beaucoup de circulation ».

questions.prompt: The French word for "traffic light" is…
questions.explanation: "le feu" (literally 'fire') is the word for a traffic light, as in « le feu est rouge »; in the plural it is les feux.
"le stationnement" means parking, the act of leaving your car somewhere, as on signs saying « stationnement interdit »; in France, le parking usually means the car park itself.
"la vitesse" means speed, how fast a vehicle goes, as in « la limite de vitesse »; it is a feminine noun.

units.title: Say It Your Way
units.description: Write the idea in French — Everyday ideas where more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Bonjour.
Bonjour, ça va ?
Bonjour à vous.
questions.explanation: "Bonjour." is the standard greeting in the morning and all day until evening; you can add « ça va ? » with people you know.

acceptableAnswers: Comment tu t'appelles ?
Tu t'appelles comment ?
C'est quoi ton prénom ?

acceptableAnswers: Je ne comprends pas.
Pardon, je ne comprends pas.
Je n'y comprends rien.
questions.explanation: "Je ne comprends pas." puts ne…pas around the verb comprends to say you do not understand; adding « Pardon » makes it more polite.

acceptableAnswers: Où est la gare ?
Pourriez-vous me dire où est la gare ?
La gare, c'est où ?

acceptableAnswers: Merci beaucoup.
Merci mille fois.
Je vous remercie vraiment.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Merci beaucoup." Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Pouvez-vous répéter ?" Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Je viens du Canada.
Je suis originaire du Canada.
Moi, je viens du Canada.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Je viens du Canada." Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
Un café, s'il vous plaît.
Puis-je avoir un café ?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît." Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Comment allez-vous ?
Comment ça va ?
Ça va bien ?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Comment allez-vous ?" Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Je vais bien, merci.
Ça va bien, merci.
Très bien, merci.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Je vais bien, merci." Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Je m'appelle Julie.
Moi, c'est Julie.
Mon nom est Julie.

acceptableAnswers: L'addition, s'il vous plaît.
Pouvez-vous apporter l'addition ?
Je voudrais l'addition, s'il vous plaît.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "L'addition, s'il vous plaît." Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Je voudrais de l'eau.
De l'eau, s'il vous plaît.
Puis-je avoir de l'eau ?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Je voudrais de l'eau." Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Quelle heure est-il ?
Vous avez l'heure ?
Il est quelle heure, s'il vous plaît ?
Quelle heure est-il, s'il vous plaît ?
Tu as l'heure ?
Il est quelle heure ?
questions.explanation: "Quelle heure est-il ?" is the standard way to ask the time; "Vous avez l'heure ?" is a common polite way to ask a stranger.

acceptableAnswers: Salut !
À bientôt !
Ciao !
Au revoir !
À plus !
questions.explanation: "Salut !" is the casual goodbye you use with a friend; « À plus ! » and « À bientôt ! » also work.

acceptableAnswers: J'ai faim.
Je meurs de faim.
J'ai vraiment faim.
questions.explanation: French says "J'ai faim." (literally 'I have hunger'), using avoir, not être; "Je meurs de faim." means 'I'm starving'.

acceptableAnswers: Où habitez-vous ?
Tu habites où ?
Où est-ce que vous habitez ?
questions.explanation: "Où habitez-vous ?" is the polite vous form for a stranger; with a friend you can say "Tu habites où ?".

acceptableAnswers: J'habite à Paris.
Je vis à Paris.
J'habite à Paris, en France.
questions.explanation: "J'habite à Paris." uses à because French puts à before the name of a city; je vis à Paris also works.

questions.prompt: Ask for directions to the bathroom.
acceptableAnswers: Où sont les toilettes ?
Pourriez-vous m'indiquer les toilettes ?
Les toilettes, s'il vous plaît ?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Où sont les toilettes ?" Everyday ideas, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Je suis désolé.
Je suis désolée.
Toutes mes excuses.

acceptableAnswers: Bonne journée !
Passez une bonne journée !
Je vous souhaite une bonne journée.
questions.explanation: "Bonne journée !" is what French speakers say when leaving someone during the day, for example in a shop; journée means the whole day.

acceptableAnswers: Combien ça coûte ?
C'est combien ?
Quel est le prix, s'il vous plaît ?

Mon français n'est pas très bon.
Je ne parle pas très bien français.

acceptableAnswers: Tu veux prendre un café ?
On va prendre un café ?
Voulez-vous prendre un café avec moi ?
questions.explanation: "Tu veux prendre un café ?" is the friendly tu form (French says prendre, 'take', a coffee); with someone you call vous, say voulez-vous prendre un café avec moi ?

acceptableAnswers: Bonne chance !
Je te souhaite bonne chance !
Je vous souhaite bonne chance !
questions.explanation: "Bonne chance !" is the direct way to wish someone good luck; bon courage ! is different and means 'hang in there'.

choices: Le dessous de l'armoire est sale.
Le dessus de l'armoire est sale.

questions.explanation: The audio says "Le dessus de l'armoire est sale." Dessus ('top') has the tight French u sound, with rounded lips, not the ou sound of dessous ('underneath').

questions.audioText: Le dessous de l'armoire est sale.
choices: Le dessous de l'armoire est sale.
Le dessus de l'armoire est sale.
Le dessus de la table est sale.

questions.audioText: Ce plat contient du poisson.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Ce plat contient du poisson.": "poisson" (fish) has a hard s sound, while "poison" has a z sound, and you hear "ce plat", not "cette boîte".

questions.audioText: Ce plat contient du poison.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Ce plat contient du poison." A single s between vowels sounds like 'z', so "poison" (poison) has a 'z' sound, while "poisson" (fish) has a double s and a hissing 's' sound.

questions.audioText: Cette boîte contient du poisson.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Cette boîte contient du poisson." The double s in "poisson" (fish) gives a hissing 's' sound, while "poison" (poison) has a single s that sounds like 'z'.

questions.audioText: Cette boîte contient du poison.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Cette boîte contient du poison." A single s between vowels sounds like 'z', so "poison" (poison) has a 'z' sound, while "poisson" (fish) has a hissing 's' sound.

questions.audioText: Ces livres sont intéressants.
choices: Ces livres ne sont pas intéressants.

choices: Ses livres ne sont pas intéressants.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Ses livres sont intéressants.": you hear the plural "ses livres sont" (not "son livre est"), the word "intéressants" and no "ne... pas".

questions.audioText: Ces photos sont anciennes.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Ces photos sont anciennes.": you hear the plural "ces photos sont" (not "cette photo est") and the word "anciennes" (old).

Nous avons vu ta mère hier.
questions.answer: Nous avons vu la mer hier.

questions.audioText: Nous avons vu ta mère hier.
choices: Nous avons vu la mer hier.
Nous avons vu ta mère hier.

questions.audioText: J'aime beaucoup le pin.

questions.audioText: Il a acheté un pin.

questions.audioText: Le cou me fait mal.

questions.audioText: Le coup me fait mal.
questions.explanation: The audio says "Le coup me fait mal." Sentences built around sounds English speakers tend to merge.

questions.audioText: Ces documents sont importants.
