units.title: Speaking: Everyday Phrases
units.description: Say it out loud — Short everyday phrases to practise saying.

questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Bonjour, comment allez-vous ?" This is the polite way to ask 'How are you?', using vous for a stranger, a customer or anyone you address formally.
Target phrase: "Bonjour, comment vas-tu ?" This means 'How are you?' and uses tu, so say it to a friend, a family member or a child.
Target phrase: "Enchanté de vous rencontrer." This means 'Pleased to meet you', with vous for polite use. A woman writes "Enchantée", which is pronounced the same.
Target phrase: "Comment tu t'appelles ?" This is the informal way to ask 'What's your name?', used with friends, children or people your age.
Target phrase: "Je m'appelle Marie." This means 'My name is Marie' (literally 'I call myself Marie'). Me shortens to m' before a vowel sound.
Target phrase: "J'ai faim." This means 'I'm hungry', but French uses avoir ('to have hunger'), not être.
Target phrase: "J'ai soif." This means 'I'm thirsty', but French uses avoir ('to have thirst'), not être.

questions.answer: Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît.
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Je voudrais un café, s'il vous plaît." "Je voudrais" ('I would like') is the polite way to order, and s'il vous plaît uses vous for a waiter or a shop.
"Où sont les toilettes ?" means "Where are the toilets?". "Toilettes" is always plural in this phrase, and the -s of "les" is silent.
"Merci beaucoup." means "Thank you very much." The final -p of "beaucoup" is silent.
"De rien." means "You're welcome." and is the usual reply to "merci". The -n of "rien" is not pronounced separately; it makes the vowel nasal.
"Excusez-moi." means "Excuse me." It is the polite vous form you use with strangers, for example to get someone's attention or to get past.
"Je suis désolé." means "I'm sorry." A woman writes "désolée", but both forms sound exactly the same.
"À bientôt !" means "See you soon!" You say it when you leave someone you expect to see again soon.
"Bonne journée !" means "Have a nice day!" People often say it when leaving a shop or saying goodbye during the day.
"Quelle heure est-il ?" means "What time is it?" Link "heure" and "est" smoothly, and run "est-il" together as "è-til".
"Il est cinq heures." means "It is five o'clock." Pronounce the -q of "cinq" and link it to "heures"; French uses "il est" for telling the time.
"J'habite à Paris." means "I live in Paris." "Je" becomes "j'" before the silent h, and you use "à" before a city name.
"Je ne comprends pas." means "I don't understand." The negation "ne ... pas" goes around the verb, and the final -ds of "comprends" is silent.
"Pouvez-vous répéter, s'il vous plaît ?" means "Can you repeat that, please?" It is a polite vous question, ideal with teachers, shop staff or strangers.
"Je suis fatigué." means "I'm tired." A woman writes "fatiguée" with an extra -e, but it sounds exactly the same.

questions.answer: Il fait très beau ce matin.
questions.explanation: "Il fait très beau ce matin." means "The weather is really nice this morning." French talks about the weather with "il fait".
"J'ai deux frères." means "I have two brothers." Je + ai shortens to "j'ai", and the final -s of "frères" is silent.
"Je parle un peu français." means "I speak a little French." After "parler" you can name the language without an article.
"Bonne chance !" means "Good luck!" "Chance" is feminine, so the adjective is "bonne".

units.title: Common Verbs (je form)
units.description: Present tense, first person — The "je" form of common verbs.

questions.explanation: The subject "je" takes the -e ending for regular -er verbs, so parler becomes "parle"; "parles", "parlent" and "parlez" belong to tu, ils and vous.
With "je", a regular -er verb like manger drops -er and adds -e, giving "mange"; the other forms go with tu, ils or nous.
The irregular verb avoir has the form "ai" for "je" (written j'ai before a vowel); "a", "avons" and "ont" go with il, nous and ils.
The irregular verb être has the form "suis" for "je"; "es" goes with tu, "sommes" with nous and "êtes" with vous.
Aller is irregular, and its "je" form is "vais"; "vas" is the tu form, "va" the il/elle form and "allez" the vous form.
The irregular verb faire has the form "fais" for "je" (and tu); "fait" is il/elle, "faisons" nous and "font" ils.
Vouloir is irregular and its "je" form is "veux"; "veut" goes with il/elle, while "voulons" and "voulez" go with nous and vous.
Pouvoir is irregular and its "je" form is "peux"; "pouvons", "pouvez" and "peuvent" go with nous, vous and ils.
questions.meaning: I can, I am able to

questions.explanation: Savoir is irregular and its "je" form is "sais"; "sait" is il/elle, "savez" vous and "savent" ils.
Prendre takes "prends" with "je" (and tu); "prend" is il/elle, "prenons" nous and "prennent" ils.
Voir takes "vois" with "je"; "voit" is il/elle, "voyons" nous and "voient" ils.
Venir is irregular and its "je" form is "viens"; "vient" goes with il/elle, "venons" with nous and "venez" with vous.
After "je", the irregular verb dire takes the form "dis" (je dis). "disons", "dites" and "disent" belong to nous, vous and ils.
Regular -ir verbs like finir take -s with "je": "finis". "finit" goes with il/elle, "finissez" with vous and "finissent" with ils/elles.
Dormir drops its -m- in the singular, so "je" takes "dors". "dort" is for il/elle, and "dormons" and "dorment" are plural forms.
questions.example: Je dors huit heures par nuit.

questions.explanation: Boire is irregular and the singular stem is "bois" (je bois). "buvons" and "buvez" are plural, and "boit" is the il/elle form.
Lire gives "lis" with "je" (je lis). "lisons", "lisez" and "lisent" are the nous, vous and ils forms.

questions.prompt: J'___ (écrire) un message à mon frère.
questions.explanation: Écrire takes "-s" after "j'": j'"écris". "écrit" is il/elle, "écrivez" is vous and "écrivent" is ils/elles.
Partir loses its final consonant in the singular and "je" takes "pars" (je pars). "part" is il/elle, while "partons" and "partent" are plural.
Mettre takes "-s" with "je": "mets" (je mets la table). "met" is il/elle, and "mettons" and "mettez" are nous and vous.
Regular -re verbs like attendre take -s with "je": j'"attends". "attend" (no -s) is il/elle, while "attendons" and "attendez" are plural.
Regular -re verbs like vendre take -s with "je": "vends". "vend" is il/elle, and "vendons" and "vendent" are plural forms.
Regular -ir verbs like choisir take -s with "je": "choisis". "choisit" is il/elle, and "choisissez" and "choisissent" are vous and ils/elles.
Comprendre follows prendre, so "je" takes "comprends" (singular stem, -s ending). "comprenons", "comprenez" and "comprennent" are the nous, vous and ils forms.
With "je", the present tense of connaître ends in -s: "connais". The forms "connaissons", "connaissez" and "connaît" belong to nous, vous and il/elle.

units.title: Food & Drink
units.description: Ordering and shopping for food — Everyday food and drink vocabulary.

questions.explanation: bread → le pain. Everyday food and drink vocabulary.
cheese → le fromage. Everyday food and drink vocabulary.
water → l'eau. Everyday food and drink vocabulary.
wine → le vin. Everyday food and drink vocabulary.
coffee → le café. Everyday food and drink vocabulary.
tea → le thé. Everyday food and drink vocabulary.
milk → le lait. Everyday food and drink vocabulary.
egg → l'œuf. Everyday food and drink vocabulary.
"Butter" in French is "le beurre", a masculine noun, as in du beurre sur le pain (butter on bread).
"Sugar" is "le sucre" (masculine). Don't mix it up with le sel, which means salt.
Salt is "le sel" in French. It is a masculine noun, so it takes "le".
Meat is "la viande" in French. It is a feminine noun, so it takes "la".
Chicken, as a dish or as the bird, is "le poulet" in French. It is masculine, so it takes "le".

questions.prompt: The French word for "fish (to eat)" is… ___
questions.explanation: Fish, both the food and the animal, is "le poisson" in French. It is masculine, so it takes "le".
Vegetable is "le légume" in French. It is masculine even though it ends in -e.
Fruit is "le fruit" in French. It has the same spelling as in English and is masculine.
Apple is "la pomme" in French. It is a feminine noun, so it takes "la".
Orange (the fruit) is "l'orange" in French. The noun is feminine and starts with a vowel, so "la" becomes "l'".
Banana is "la banane" in French. It is a feminine noun, so it takes "la".
Potato is "la pomme de terre" in French, literally "apple of the earth". It is feminine, like "pomme".
"le riz" is the French word for rice; riz is a masculine noun, so it takes le.
"la soupe" is the French word for soup; soupe is a feminine noun, so it takes la.
"Cake" is "le gâteau". Note the accent on the â and the plural with -x: des gâteaux.
"Juice" is "le jus", with a silent s, as in un jus d'orange (an orange juice).
"Breakfast", the morning meal, is "le petit-déjeuner". Literally it means a "small lunch" (déjeuner = lunch).

units.title: Directions & Places
units.description: Finding your way in French — Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.

questions.explanation: "droite" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.
"gauche" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.
"droit" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.

questions.prompt: Le café est en ___ de la poste.
questions.explanation: "face" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.
"près" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.
"loin" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.
"gare" means train station, which is the place the clue asks for; poste, banque and place are other places in town.

questions.prompt: L'___ de bus est au coin de la rue.
questions.explanation: "arrêt" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.

questions.prompt: La pharmacie est à ___ de la boulangerie.
questions.explanation: "côté" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.
questions.meaning: side; à côté de = next to

questions.explanation: "derrière" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.

questions.prompt: Le parc est juste ___ la mairie. (in front of)
questions.explanation: "devant" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.
"rue" means street, as the clue asks; route is a road between towns, and place and plage are a square and a beach.
"carrefour" means crossroads, as the clue asks; feu is a traffic light and rond-point is a roundabout.

questions.prompt: Attendez que le ___ passe au vert.
questions.explanation: Only a traffic light turns green, so "feu" fits "passe au vert"; a crossroads, bridge or pavement cannot change colour.

questions.prompt: Traversez le ___ pour arriver au centre-ville.
questions.explanation: You cross a bridge to reach the town centre, and "pont" is masculine like "le"; a traffic light, sign or map is not something you cross.
Counting exits ("la deuxième sortie") describes a roundabout, so "rond-point" is right; a crossroads, traffic light or bridge has no numbered exits.

questions.prompt: La ___ principale est très animée le samedi.
questions.explanation: A main town square is busy on Saturdays, and "place" is feminine like "La ... principale"; the other nouns are masculine.
A building has an entrance that can be closed, so "entrée" fits "du bâtiment est fermée"; an avenue, address or arrival cannot be closed.

questions.prompt: Utilisez la ___ de secours en cas d'urgence.
questions.explanation: "sortie" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.

questions.prompt: Le magasin est juste au ___ de la rue.
questions.explanation: "au coin de la rue" is the set phrase for 'at the corner of the street', so "coin" is right; a bridge, pavement or plan has no 'of the street' sense here.

questions.prompt: Regarde la ___ pour trouver le chemin.
questions.explanation: You look at a map to find your way, so "carte" is right; a street, a station or a square cannot be consulted to find the route.

questions.prompt: Je suis complètement ___ dans cette ville.
questions.explanation: "perdu" is correct here. Everyday vocabulary for asking and giving directions.

questions.prompt: Quelle est votre ___ exacte ? – 12, rue Victor Hugo.
questions.explanation: "adresse" is the French word for a postal address, matching the clue "(address)"; "position", "direction" and "rue" are also feminine, so only the meaning picks it out.
"quartier" means a neighbourhood and is masculine, matching "un"; "ville", "place" and "rue" are feminine and would need "une".
"direction" is the noun used in the set phrase "dans quelle direction" (in which direction) when asking which way to go. Rue, gare and ville are places, not ways to head.

units.title: Weather & Seasons
units.description: Talking about the weather — Everyday weather vocabulary and expressions.

questions.prompt: Il fait beau ___ : le soleil brille depuis ce matin.
questions.explanation: "aujourd'hui" fits because "le soleil brille depuis ce matin" describes today so far; "demain" and "hier" are other days, and "ce soir" has not come yet.

questions.prompt: Les feuilles tombent des arbres en ___.
questions.explanation: Leaves fall from the trees in autumn, so "automne" is right. Note that you say "en automne", "en hiver" and "en été", but "au printemps".
"chaud" is used after "il fait" to describe heat, and summer is hot. Froid, glacial and gelé all describe cold, which does not fit "en été".
"froid" is used after "il fait" to describe cold weather, which fits winter. Torride, chaud and étouffant all describe heat.
"nuageux" describes a sky full of clouds, matching the clue "cloudy". Ensoleillé, clair and dégagé all describe a sky without clouds.

questions.prompt: Il y a du ___ ce matin.
questions.explanation: "vent" is masculine and starts with a consonant, so it takes the partitive "du" in "il y a du vent". Pluie and neige are feminine ("de la"), and orage needs "de l'".
Snow falls in the coldest season, and "hiver" is winter, which takes "en". Été, juillet and automne do not fit, and juillet is a month ("en juillet" would not mean a season).

questions.prompt: Le ___ annonce de la pluie demain.
questions.explanation: "bulletin" is correct here. Everyday weather vocabulary and expressions.
questions.example: Le bulletin météo annonce de la pluie demain.

questions.explanation: "magnifique" means wonderful, matching the clue, and is the only positive word here. Épouvantable, affreux and horrible all mean awful.
Temperature is measured in "degrés", so "vingt degrés" means twenty degrees. Heures, kilos and mètres measure time, weight and length.

questions.prompt: Il y a du ___ sur la route.
questions.explanation: "brouillard" is masculine, so it takes "du" (du brouillard). "Pluie" and "neige" are feminine and need "de la", and "orage" needs "un".
After "il va" you need an infinitive, and an umbrella is for rain, so "pleuvoir" (to rain) is right. "Neiger" is snow, not what an umbrella is for.
The sun rises early in summer, and the verb for rising is "se lève". "Se couche" means it sets, which would go with late, not early.
"temps" is correct here. Everyday weather vocabulary and expressions.
A clear sky is "dégagé", meaning free of clouds. "Nuageux", "couvert" and "gris" all describe a cloudy sky, the opposite.

questions.prompt: Il y a eu un orage avec des ___. (lightning)
questions.explanation: A storm brings lightning, which is "éclairs" in French. "Flocons" are snowflakes and "vagues" are waves, which do not belong to an orage.

questions.prompt: La météo prévoit une ___ de chaleur. (wave)
questions.explanation: A heatwave is a "vague de chaleur", a fixed phrase using "vague". "Saison", "journée" and "semaine" do not combine with "de chaleur" this way.
The subject "les feuilles" is plural, so the verb takes the third-person plural ending: "tombent". "Tombe" is singular and "tomber" is the infinitive.
To say the wind blows hard, French uses "fort" as an adverb after the verb: "le vent souffle fort". "Bon", "beau" and "long" do not describe how wind blows.

questions.prompt: Il fait un froid ___ ce matin.
questions.explanation: "glacial" is correct here. Everyday weather vocabulary and expressions.
A sky that is "couvert de" something is covered with clouds, so "nuages" is right. Degrees, days and seasons cannot cover the sky.

questions.prompt: Les fleurs sortent et il fait doux. C'est quelle saison ? ___
questions.explanation: Flowers coming back, trees turning green and mild weather describe spring, "printemps"; in summer it is hot, and autumn and winter bring falling leaves and cold.
questions.example: Au printemps, il fait souvent doux.

questions.prompt: La pluie a duré toute la ___ (de 8 h à 18 h).
questions.explanation: After "toute la" you need a feminine noun, and "journée" is the one that means the whole day; "soir", "jour" and "matin" are masculine, so they need "tout le".
Freezing weather happens in the cold winter month of "janvier"; août, juillet and mai are warm months, so they don't go with "il gèle".

questions.prompt: Le climat ici est très ___. (le contraire de « sec »)
questions.explanation: The clue asks for the opposite of "sec" (dry), which is "humide" (damp); "froid" and "chaud" describe temperature, not dryness.

units.title: Opposites
units.description: Common adjective pairs — Learn everyday adjectives with their opposites, like grand and petit.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "grand" in French is…
questions.explanation: Grand means big or tall, so its opposite is "petit", meaning small or short.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "chaud" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: Chaud means hot, so its opposite is "froid", meaning cold.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "rapide" in French is…
questions.explanation: Rapide means fast, so its opposite is "lent", meaning slow (feminine: lente).

questions.prompt: The opposite of "facile" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: Facile means easy, so its opposite is "difficile", meaning difficult. It has the same form for masculine and feminine.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "propre" in French is…
questions.explanation: Propre means clean, so its opposite is "sale", meaning dirty.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "plein" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: Plein means full, so its opposite is "vide", meaning empty, as in un verre vide (an empty glass).

questions.prompt: The opposite of "riche" in French is…
questions.explanation: Riche means rich, so its opposite is "pauvre", meaning poor.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "jeune" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: "vieux" (old) is the opposite of "jeune" (young); its feminine is "vieille", and it becomes "vieil" before a masculine noun starting with a vowel.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "fort" in French is…
questions.explanation: "faible" (weak) is the opposite of "fort" (strong): they describe opposite levels of strength.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "heureux" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: "triste" (sad) is the opposite of "heureux" (happy): they describe opposite feelings.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "beau" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: "laid" (ugly) is the opposite of "beau" (beautiful): they describe opposite appearances.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "ouvert" in French is…
questions.explanation: "fermé" (closed) is the opposite of "ouvert" (open): a door or a shop is either one or the other.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "haut" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: "bas" (low) is the opposite of "haut" (high): they describe opposite heights.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "long" in French is…
questions.explanation: "court" (short) is the opposite of "long" (long): they describe opposite lengths.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "cher" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: "bon marché" (cheap) is the opposite of "cher" (expensive), and it never changes form: une robe bon marché.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "lourd" in French is…
questions.explanation: "léger" (light) is the opposite of "lourd" (heavy): they describe opposite weights.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "dur" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: "mou" (soft) is the opposite of "dur" (hard): they describe opposite textures, like a hard bed versus a soft one.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "clair" in French is…
questions.explanation: For colours, "foncé" (dark) is the opposite of "clair" (light), as in bleu clair versus bleu foncé.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "calme" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: "bruyant" (noisy) is the opposite of "calme" (quiet, calm): they describe opposite levels of noise, as in une rue calme versus une rue bruyante.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "gentil" in French is…
questions.explanation: "méchant" (mean, nasty) is the opposite of "gentil" (kind): they describe opposite ways of treating people.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "poli" in French is…
questions.explanation: "impoli" (rude) is the opposite of "poli" (polite): French often forms opposites with the prefix im- or in-.

questions.prompt: The opposite of "gros" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: Describing a person, "mince" (slim) is the opposite of "gros" (fat, big).

questions.prompt: The opposite of "sec" in French is…
questions.explanation: "mouillé" (wet) is the opposite of "sec" (dry), as in "une serviette mouillée" (a wet towel).

questions.prompt: The opposite of "tôt" in French is… ___
questions.explanation: "tard" (late) is the opposite of "tôt" (early); both are adverbs, so they never change form, as in "Je me couche tard."

questions.prompt: The opposite of "neuf" in French is…
questions.explanation: For objects, "usé" (worn out) is the opposite of "neuf" (brand new), as in des chaussures neuves versus des chaussures usées.

units.title: Reflexive Verbs & Daily Routine
units.description: Talking about your day — Present-tense reflexive verbs for daily routines.

questions.explanation: The subject "je" takes the reflexive pronoun "me" (elided before the vowel in "réveille") with the -e verb ending: "me réveille".
The subject "tu" takes the pronoun "te" and the -s ending, with the accent from "lever": "te lèves".
The subject "il" takes the pronoun "se" and the singular ending -e: "se lave"; "se lavent" would need a plural subject.
The subject "nous" takes the reflexive pronoun "nous" and the ending -ons: "nous habillons".
The subject "vous" takes the reflexive pronoun "vous" and the ending -ez: "vous brossez".
The plural subject "elles" takes "se" and the plural ending -ent: "se coiffent"; "se coiffe" is singular.
The subject "je" takes the reflexive pronoun "me" and the ending -e: "me douche".
The subject "tu" takes the pronoun "te" and the ending -s: "te rases".
The subject "il" is singular, so the verb takes "se" and the ending -e: "se repose"; "se reposent" is plural.
The subject "Nous" takes the reflexive pronoun "nous" and the -ons ending: "nous promenons". The other options use pronouns for me, vous or il.

questions.prompt: Vous ___ (se dépêcher) pour ne pas être en retard.
questions.explanation: The subject "Vous" needs the matching pronoun "vous" and the -ez ending: "vous dépêchez". Forms with se or te belong to other subjects.
"Elles" is third person plural, so the pronoun is "se" and the verb ends in -ent: "se couchent".
"Je" requires the pronoun "me", which elides to m' before the vowel in habitue: "m'habitue".
"Tu" goes with the pronoun "te" and a verb ending in -s: "te souviens".
"Il" takes the pronoun "se", which elides to s' before appelle: "s'appelle". The other options use pronouns for other subjects.
With "Nous" the verb takes the pronoun "nous" and the -ons ending, and ennuyer keeps y in the nous form: "nous ennuyons".
The subject "Vous" requires the pronoun "vous" and the -ez ending: "vous sentez".
"Elles" is plural, so the verb needs the -ent ending with the pronoun se: "se disputent". "se dispute" is singular.
"Je" takes the pronoun "me", elided to m' before the vowel: "m'occupe".
questions.meaning: I look after, I take care of

questions.explanation: "Tu" pairs with the pronoun "te" and a verb ending in -s: "te maquilles".
"Il" takes the pronoun "se" and the irregular singular form of se plaindre, with no -e or -s ending: "se plaint".
With the subject "Nous" the reflexive pronoun is also nous and the verb ends in -ons, so the blank takes "nous amusons": "Nous nous amusons".
questions.meaning: we have fun, we enjoy ourselves

questions.explanation: The subject "Vous" requires the reflexive pronoun "vous" and the -ez ending, giving "vous inquiétez" for s'inquiéter.
The plural subject "Elles" needs the third-person plural reflexive form "s'endorment" (s'endormir: ils/elles s'endorment).
The subject "Je" takes the reflexive pronoun "me" and the first-person ending -s, giving "me détends" for se détendre.

units.title: Aller + Infinitive (Near Future)
units.description: Talking about what's about to happen — Futur proche: aller + infinitive.

lessons.title: Aller + Infinitive (Near Future) 1
lessons.subtitle: Talking about plans and what's going to happen

questions.explanation: With the subject "Je", aller is conjugated as "vais", followed by the infinitive "manger" to say what is about to happen.
The subject "Tu" requires the form "vas" of aller before the infinitive "partir" in the near future.
The singular subject "Il" takes "va" (il va), followed by the infinitive "étudier" to express the near future.
The subject "Nous" takes "allons" (nous allons) before the infinitive "voyager" for a planned future action.
The subject "Vous" takes "allez" (vous allez) before the infinitive "arriver".

lessons.title: Aller + Infinitive (Near Future) 2
lessons.subtitle: Talking about plans and what's going to happen

questions.explanation: The plural subject "Elles" takes "vont" (elles vont) before the infinitive "venir" in the near future.
The subject "Je" takes "vais" (je vais), followed by the infinitive "acheter" to say what you are about to do.
The subject "Tu" takes "vas" (tu vas), followed by the infinitive "regarder" for the near future.
The subject "Il" takes the third-person singular of aller, so "va" goes before the infinitive "finir" to say what he is about to do.
The subject "Nous" takes the first-person plural of aller, "allons", followed by the infinitive "déjeuner" to express the near future.

lessons.title: Aller + Infinitive (Near Future) 3
lessons.subtitle: Talking about plans and what's going to happen

questions.explanation: The subject "Vous" takes the second-person plural form of aller, "allez", followed by the infinitive "prendre".
The plural subject "Elles" takes the third-person plural of aller, "vont", before the infinitive "rester".
The subject "Je" takes the first-person singular of aller, "vais", followed by the infinitive "appeler" for something about to happen.
The subject "Tu" takes the second-person singular of aller, "vas", followed by the infinitive "faire".
The subject "Il" takes the third-person singular of aller, "va", and "dormir" stays in the infinitive to say what he is going to do tonight.

lessons.title: Aller + Infinitive (Near Future) 4
lessons.subtitle: Talking about plans and what's going to happen

questions.explanation: The subject "Nous" takes the first-person plural of aller, "allons", followed by the infinitive "visiter".
The subject "Vous" takes the form "allez", followed by the infinitive "commencer" to ask what is about to start.
The plural subject "Elles" needs the third-person plural of aller, "vont", before the infinitive "chanter".
The subject "Je" takes "vais", the first-person singular of aller, followed by the infinitive "écrire".
The subject "Tu" takes the second-person singular of aller, "vas", before the infinitive "lire" for a near-future plan.

lessons.title: Aller + Infinitive (Near Future) 5
lessons.subtitle: Talking about plans and what's going to happen

questions.explanation: The subject "Il" is third person singular, so aller becomes "va" before the infinitive jouer.
With "Nous" the verb aller is "allons", followed by the infinitive sortir to express the near future.
The subject "Vous" takes the form "allez" of aller, followed by the infinitive répondre.
"Elles" is third person plural, so aller becomes "vont" before the infinitive apprendre.
With "Je" the verb aller is "vais" (not "vas", which goes with tu), followed by the infinitive essayer.

units.title: Health & the Body
units.description: At the doctor's — Health, symptoms, and visiting the doctor.

questions.explanation: "tête" is feminine, so it takes "à la"; ventre, dos and bras are masculine and would need "au".
"au" is à + le, so the body part must be masculine: "ventre" fits, while tête, gorge and jambe are feminine and take "à la".
A doctor gives you an "ordonnance" (a written prescription) that you take to the pharmacy; the other words are masculine or not something handed over.

questions.prompt: Je dois prendre ce ___ trois fois par jour.
questions.explanation: You take "ce médicament" (medicine) three times a day; "ce" needs a masculine noun and only "médicament" is something you swallow.
"de la" needs a feminine noun, and "fièvre" (fever) is the symptom you can have for a day; dos, rhume and mal are masculine.
"un gros" requires a masculine noun, and "rhume" (a cold) is the only masculine illness here; fièvre, toux and grippe are feminine.

questions.prompt: Il tousse et a mal à la ___.
questions.explanation: Coughing goes with a sore "gorge" (throat), and "à la" needs a feminine noun, unlike ventre, dos and bras.

questions.prompt: Le docteur va m'___. (listen to my chest)
questions.explanation: "ausculter" means to listen to someone's chest with a stethoscope, as the clue says; the other verbs (put to sleep, operate on, dress) do not match.

questions.prompt: J'ai mal aux dents, alors j'ai pris rendez-vous chez le ___.
questions.explanation: Teeth are looked after by a "dentiste"; a cardiologue treats the heart, a pharmacien sells medicine, and a médecin is a general doctor.
"piqûre" is correct here. Health, symptoms, and visiting the doctor.
After "le" you need a masculine noun, and "bras" is masculine (le bras); "jambe" and "tête" are feminine, and "main" is feminine too, so "le" cannot precede them.
"au" means "à le", so a masculine noun is needed: "dos" is masculine, while "main", "tête" and "jambe" are feminine and would need "à la".

questions.prompt: J'ai besoin d'un ___ pour la douleur.

units.title: Prepositions of Time
units.description: Talking about when things happen — Common prepositions used to talk about time.

questions.explanation: "avant" means "before" a moment in time, as in "avant le dîner" (before dinner); "pendant" means "during" and "depuis" means "since".
"après" means "after" and comes before the event, as in "après le dîner" (after dinner).
"pendant" means "during" and comes before a period of time, as in "pendant les vacances" (during the holidays).
"depuis" means "since" for a starting point that still continues now, as in "J'habite ici depuis lundi" (I've lived here since Monday).
"jusqu'à" means "until", as in "jusqu'à midi" (until noon); with a masculine noun it becomes "jusqu'au".

questions.prompt: Choose the right word: Hier soir, j'ai dormi ___ huit heures.

questions.explanation: "en" is used before months and years to mean "in", as in "en juillet" or "en 2020"; "vers" means "around" and "après" means "after".

questions.prompt: The French word for "on (a day)" is…
questions.explanation: Before a date or a regular weekday, French uses the article "le" where English says "on": "le 14 juillet" (on 14 July), "le lundi" (on Mondays). For one particular day, French often uses no word at all: "lundi".

questions.prompt: The French word for "at (a time)" is… ___

questions.prompt: The French word for "not yet" is…

questions.explanation: "d'abord" is the adverb for "at first" or "first of all" and often starts a sequence, as in "D'abord, on mange."

"pas" is correct here. Common negative structures beyond ne...pas.
The clue "no longer" calls for "plus" in "ne ... plus": "Nous n'avons plus le temps" (We no longer have the time).
The clue "nothing" calls for "rien", which replaces the thing done: "Ils ne font rien le week-end" (They do nothing at the weekend).
The clue "never" calls for "jamais" in "ne ... jamais": "Je ne vais jamais au cinéma" (I never go to the cinema).
"pas" is correct here. Common negative structures beyond ne...pas.

questions.prompt: Il n'y a ___ dans la salle. (nobody)
questions.explanation: "Il n'y a personne" is the fixed way to say nobody is there, and the clue "nobody" points to "personne".
The clue "(not)" asks for the basic negation, so "pas" completes ne...pas. The other words would mean never, nothing or no longer.

questions.prompt: Nous ne mangeons ___ de sucre. (no more)
questions.explanation: The clue "(no more)" means 'no longer', which in French is ne...plus. So "plus" fits: Nous ne mangeons plus de sucre.
The clue "(nothing)" is expressed by ne...rien, placed after the verb. So "rien" completes Vous ne savez rien.
The clue "(never)" is expressed by ne...jamais. So "jamais" gives Elles ne viennent jamais le lundi.
The clue "(not)" asks for the plain negation ne...pas, and de follows it as usual in a negative sentence. So "pas" is right.
The clue "(nothing)" means ne...rien, which sits between the auxiliary and the participle. So "rien" gives Il n'a rien compris.
The clue "(never)" is expressed by ne...jamais. So "jamais" gives Nous n'irons jamais là-bas.
"pas" is correct here. Common negative structures beyond ne...pas.
The clue "(nothing)" is expressed by ne...rien after the verb. So "rien" gives Elle ne mange rien.
The clue "(not)" asks for the basic negation, and d'amis after it shows the usual ne...pas de pattern. So "pas" is right.
The clue "(never)" is expressed by ne...jamais, and de follows it before a noun. So "jamais" gives Je ne bois jamais d'alcool.
The clue "(no longer)" is expressed by ne...plus, meaning 'not any more'. So "plus" gives Nous ne faisons plus ça.

units.title: Question Formation
units.description: Asking questions — Forming questions with est-ce que and inversion.

questions.explanation: The yes/no question marker is "Est"-ce que, so the blank takes "Est" before "-ce que"; "Que", "Qui" and "Où" cannot start this fixed phrase.
questions.meaning: first word of the question phrase 'est-ce que'

questions.explanation: The fixed question phrase is est-ce "que", followed by a full statement ("vous êtes prêts"); "qui", "quoi" and "où" don't complete it.
With inverted "-vous", the verb must be the vous form of aller: "allez" (comment allez-vous ?). "Vais" and "vas" belong to je and tu.
The inverted subject "-il" is third person singular, so aller takes the form "va" (où va-t-il ?); "vais", "vont" and "allons" go with other subjects.
questions.example: Où va-t-il ?

questions.explanation: The inverted subject "-vous" requires the vous form of vouloir: "voulez" (que voulez-vous faire ?). The other forms belong to tu, il or nous.
The inverted subject "-elle" is third person singular, so aller takes "va" (va-t-elle arriver ?, with the added -t- between vowels); "vas" and "vais" don't match elle.
questions.example: Quand va-t-elle arriver ?

questions.explanation: The inverted subject "-tu" takes the tu form of être: "es" (pourquoi es-tu triste ?). "Suis", "est" and "êtes" go with je, il and vous.
"Qui est-ce ?" is the fixed question for identifying someone, using the third-person form "est" with the inverted "-ce"; the other forms of être don't fit "ce".
The subject "tu" needs the passé composé with avoir in the tu form: "as vu" (tu as vu). "A vu", "avez vu" and "ai vu" go with il, vous and je.
The verb "avez" is the vous form of avoir, so the inverted pronoun must be "vous" (avez-vous compris ?); tu, nous and je need other verb forms.
After est-ce qu'"il", the verb is third person singular, so habiter is "habite" (est-ce qu'il habite ici ?); "habites", "habitent" and "habitons" match other subjects.
"Puis" is the first person singular of pouvoir, so the inverted subject must be "je" (puis-je vous aider ?); il, tu and nous would need other verb forms.
Inversion puts the subject pronoun after the verb, and the polite 'you' here is "vous": Voulez-vous... ? The verb ending "-ez" matches "vous".
The subject is "nous", so "sommes" (we are) is the matching form of être; "suis" goes with je, "êtes" with vous and "sont" with ils/elles.
The verb "sais" is the tu form of savoir; the vous form would be "savez", so only "tu" fits Sais-___ where il est ?
The subject "elles" is third-person plural, so venir takes "viennent"; "vient" is singular, "venons" is nous and "venez" is vous.
The subject is "ce livre" (this book), which is third-person singular, so the verb is "coûte"; the other forms go with tu, nous or a plural subject.
questions.example: Combien ça coûte ?

questions.explanation: The fixed question for asking the time is Quelle heure est-il ?, using "est" (is) with the impersonal il.
After the conjugated verb "peux" (can), the next verb stays in the infinitive, so "partir" is needed, not a conjugated form or the participle.
This is the passé composé (avez + past participle), so the blank needs the participle "lu" from lire, not the infinitive or a present form.
The subject is "ça" (singular), so plaire takes the third-person singular "plaît"; "plaisent" is plural and "plais" is for je/tu.
questions.example: Est-ce que ça te plaît ?

questions.explanation: With the subject "vous" the verb être is "êtes", as in Où êtes-vous né ? (where were you born).
In the passé composé, dire takes avoir, and with the subject "il" the auxiliary is "a": Qu'est-ce qu'il a dit ? (with inversion: Qu'a-t-il dit ?).
questions.example: Qu'a-t-il dit ?

questions.explanation: The subject is "tu", so être takes the form "es"; "suis" is je, "est" is il and "êtes" is vous.
The verb ending "-ez" in "Aimez" goes with "vous", and in an inverted question the pronoun follows the verb with a hyphen: "Aimez-vous voyager ?"

units.title: Adverbs of Frequency
units.description: Saying how often — Adverbs and expressions of frequency.

questions.explanation: always → toujours. Adverbs and expressions of frequency.
usually → généralement. Adverbs and expressions of frequency.
often → souvent. Adverbs and expressions of frequency.
"parfois" means "sometimes"; "jamais" is never, "presque jamais" is almost never and "régulièrement" is regularly.
occasionally → de temps en temps. Adverbs and expressions of frequency.
rarely → rarement. Adverbs and expressions of frequency.
never → jamais. Adverbs and expressions of frequency.

questions.prompt: The French word for "every day" is…
questions.explanation: every day → tous les jours. Adverbs and expressions of frequency.

questions.prompt: The French word for "every week" is… ___
questions.explanation: "toutes les semaines" means 'every week' (literally 'all the weeks'); "chaque mois" is every month, and the others give no fixed interval.

questions.prompt: The French word for "every month" is…
questions.explanation: "tous les mois" means "every month": "tous les" plus a plural time word gives "every", so "tous les jours" would be every day.
"une fois" means one time (once), built from fois (time, occasion), as in « Je vais au cinéma une fois par mois ». "toujours" means always and "tous les jours" means every day.
"deux fois" literally means two times, which is how French says twice, as in « Je l'appelle deux fois par semaine ». The other options are general frequency words, not a count.

questions.prompt: The French word for "several times" is…
questions.explanation: "plusieurs fois" means several times: "plusieurs" is several and "fois" is the word for an occurrence (times), unlike "souvent" (often).

questions.prompt: The French word for "from time to time" is… ___
questions.explanation: "de temps à autre" means 'from time to time', a slightly more formal twin of 'de temps en temps'; "rarement" means seldom, not occasionally.
"constamment" means 'constantly', all the time without stopping; it is built like the English word, with -amment matching '-antly'.
"régulièrement" is régulier plus the adverb ending -ment, just like regular plus -ly in English. "rarement" means rarely, the opposite idea.
"fréquemment" comes from fréquent; adjectives ending in -ent form their adverb with -emment. "de temps à autre" means from time to time, which is less often.
seldom → peu souvent. Adverbs and expressions of frequency.

questions.prompt: The French word for "every year" is…
questions.explanation: "chaque année" means 'every year' (chaque = each, année = year); "chaque semaine" would be every week.
"quotidiennement" means 'daily', from quotidien (everyday); in casual speech people often say 'tous les jours'.
"chaque semaine" means 'each week', which is how French says 'weekly'; the other options are not tied to a week.
"chaque mois" means 'each month', so it gives the 'monthly' interval; "régulièrement" only means regularly.

questions.prompt: The French word for "almost never" is… ___
questions.explanation: "presque jamais" means 'almost never' (presque = almost, jamais = never); "de temps en temps" means from time to time.

questions.prompt: The French word for "almost always" is…
questions.explanation: "presque toujours" means 'almost always' (presque = almost, toujours = always); "rarement" is the opposite.

questions.prompt: The French word for "once a week" is… ___
questions.explanation: "une fois par semaine" literally means 'one time per week', which is 'once a week'; "tous les mois" would be every month.

units.title: Sports & Leisure Activities
units.description: Talking about sport — Common sports and leisure vocabulary.

questions.explanation: "le football" is masculine, like most borrowed sport names, and is often shortened to 'le foot' in everyday French.
French borrowed the English word, and it is masculine, so it is "le basketball" (often shortened to "le basket").
Tennis was borrowed unchanged into French and is masculine, so it is "le tennis"; you say "jouer au tennis".
"la natation" is the noun for the sport of swimming; the verb "to swim" is "nager".
"la course" is the noun for running as a sport (in full "la course à pied"); the verb "to run" is "courir".
Sport names ending in -isme are masculine, so cycling is "le cyclisme", built on "cycle" (bike).
"le ski" names both the skis and the sport of skiing; "to go skiing" is "faire du ski".
Golf was borrowed unchanged from English and is masculine, so it is "le golf"; you say "jouer au golf".
French borrowed the English word as a masculine noun, so it is "le volleyball", often shortened to "le volley".
Boxing is feminine in French and spelled with -xe, so it is "la boxe"; you say "faire de la boxe".
The English ending -ics often becomes -ique in French, and the noun is feminine: "la gymnastique" (often shortened to "la gym").
Yoga keeps its name in French and is masculine, so it is "le yoga"; you say "faire du yoga".
Climbing is the feminine noun escalade (from "escalader", to climb), and "la" becomes l' before a vowel, giving "l'escalade".
"le surf" is borrowed straight from English and is masculine, so it takes "le"; "le ski" is skiing and "le yoga" is yoga.
"le rugby" is spelled just as in English and is masculine, so it takes "le".
"le handball" is borrowed from English, written as one word and masculine; "le basketball" is basketball.
Athletics is "l'athlétisme": the masculine "le" becomes "l'" before the vowel, and note the accent on "é".
A team is "l'équipe", a feminine noun: "la" becomes "l'" before the vowel. "Le stade" is the place where a team plays.
A sports match is "le match", borrowed from English and masculine; "l'entraîneur" is the coach.
A coach is "l'entraîneur", the person who trains a team or an athlete; it comes from the verb s'entraîner (to train).
A stadium is "le stade", the big outdoor venue for matches; "la salle de sport" is an indoor gym.
A gym where you work out is "la salle de sport"; "la piscine" is a swimming pool and "la patinoire" is an ice rink.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to train" is…
questions.explanation: To train is "s'entraîner", a reflexive verb, as in Je m'entraîne le lundi; "marquer" means to score.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to win" is… ___
questions.explanation: To win is "gagner"; its opposite, "perdre", means to lose.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to lose" is…
questions.explanation: To lose is "perdre", the opposite of gagner; "marquer" means to score and "jouer" means to play.

units.title: At Work / Office Vocabulary
units.description: Talking about your job — Everyday office and workplace vocabulary.

questions.explanation: "le bureau" is the office, the room or place where you work; the same word also means a desk.
"la réunion" is a meeting, when colleagues get together to discuss work; "le projet" is a project and "le patron" is the boss.

questions.prompt: The French word for "colleague (at work)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "le collègue" is someone you work alongside; "l'employé" just means anyone who works for a company.
"le patron" is the boss, the person who runs the business or manages you; "l'équipe" is the team.
"l'employé" is a person who works for a company; "le patron" is the boss who employs them.
"le salaire" is the money you are paid for your work; "le rapport" is a report.

questions.prompt: The French word for "schedule (work hours)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "l'horaire" is your schedule, the hours you work; "le bureau" is the office.
"la date limite" is the deadline, literally the 'limit date' by which the work must be finished.
"le projet" is the French word for a project and is masculine, as in « Nous travaillons sur un nouveau projet ». "le rapport" is a report.

questions.prompt: The French word for "email (at work)" is…
questions.explanation: "le courriel" is the official French word for an email; in everyday speech in France people often say "le mail".
"le rapport" is a written report, as in « Je dois finir le rapport ce soir ». "le courriel" is an email, not a report.
"le contrat" is a contract. Note the spelling: there is no c before the t, unlike English contract.
"l'entretien" is the word for a job interview, as in « J'ai un entretien demain ». A media interview is usually une interview.
"le CV" (curriculum vitae) is what French speakers call a résumé, and it is masculine. You send it before an entretien.
"la promotion" looks like the English word and means moving up to a better job; note that it is feminine, so it takes "la".
"les vacances" means vacation or holidays and is always plural in this sense, as in « Je pars en vacances en août ».
"la pause" is a short break from work, as in « On fait une pause café ? ». It is feminine.
"la tâche" means a task or job to do and is feminine. Keep the circumflex: without it, la tache means a stain.

questions.prompt: The French word for "team (at work)" is…
questions.explanation: "l'équipe" means the team, the group of people you work with; it is feminine (une équipe) and elides to l' before the vowel.
"Client" is spelled the same in French, and it is masculine, so it takes "le": "le client" (a female client is "la cliente").
"la présentation" means a presentation; it is feminine and is spelled with an accent on the first e.

questions.prompt: The French word for "computer (at the office)" is…
questions.explanation: A computer is "l'ordinateur"; it is masculine (un ordinateur), and "le" becomes "l'" before the vowel.

questions.prompt: The French word for "printer (at the office)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "l'imprimante" is the printer, from the verb imprimer (to print); it is feminine and takes l' because it starts with a vowel.

questions.prompt: The French word for "to hire" is…
questions.explanation: "To hire" is "embaucher"; don't confuse it with its opposite, licencier (to fire).

questions.prompt: The French word for "to resign" is… ___
questions.explanation: To leave your job by choice is "démissionner" (the noun is la démission, a resignation).

units.title: City & Public Transport
units.description: Getting around town — City and public-transport vocabulary.

questions.explanation: "City" or "town" is "la ville", a feminine noun; the town centre is le centre-ville.
A street is "la rue", a feminine noun, as in « J'habite rue Victor-Hugo ».
"l'avenue" is spelled like the English word, but it is feminine, so "la" elides to "l'" before the vowel. "la rue" is the general word for a street.
A town square is "la place"; careful, it does not mean "place" in the English sense, and a square shape is un carré.
A bridge is "le pont", a masculine noun, as in le pont Neuf in Paris.
"le bâtiment" is the general word for any building. "la station de métro" is a metro station, "le marché" a market and "la ville" a town or city.
"le quartier" is a neighbourhood, a district within a town. "le piéton" is a pedestrian and "le pont" a bridge.
"le trottoir" is the raised path beside the road where people walk (the pavement). "le passage piéton" is the striped crossing over the road.

questions.prompt: The French word for "traffic light (in the city)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "le feu" also means fire, but in a street it means the traffic light (short for "feu de signalisation"), as in "le feu est rouge".
"le rond-point" is the roundabout where cars drive round a circle; literally it means "round point". "le passage piéton" is a pedestrian crossing.

questions.prompt: The French word for "bus stop" is…
questions.explanation: "l'arrêt de bus" comes from "arrêter" (to stop): it is where the bus stops. "arrêt" starts with a vowel, so "le" becomes "l'".

questions.prompt: The French word for "subway station" is… ___
questions.explanation: "la station de métro" is an underground (subway) station; French uses "station" for the metro and "gare" for trains. "le sens unique" is a one-way street.

questions.prompt: The French word for "ticket machine" is…
questions.explanation: "le distributeur de billets" is a machine that hands out (distribue) tickets; the same phrase is also used for a cash machine. "le trottoir" is the sidewalk.

questions.prompt: The French word for "map (street plan)" is… ___
questions.explanation: "le plan" is a street map of a town or metro network; a map of a country is "une carte". "la banlieue" is the suburbs.

questions.prompt: The French word for "town hall" is…
questions.explanation: "la mairie" is the town hall, the office of the mayor (le maire). "la banlieue" is the suburbs and "le feu" a traffic light.
A park is "le parc", spelled with a c and masculine; it does not mean a car park, which is un parking.
A library is "la bibliothèque"; la librairie is a false friend and means a bookshop.
A church is "l'église", a feminine noun; "la" becomes "l'" before the vowel.
"le marché" is a market where stalls sell food and goods. "la mairie" is the town hall and "le pont" a bridge.
"la banlieue" is the residential area around a big city, the suburbs. "le parc" is a park, "le feu" a traffic light and "la rue" a street.
"le centre-ville" is the central part of a town, with its shops and offices: downtown. "la banlieue" is the suburbs and "le rond-point" a roundabout.

questions.prompt: The French word for "traffic jam" is…
questions.explanation: "l'embouteillage" is a traffic jam, when cars are stuck and barely move. "le plan" is a map and "le quartier" a neighbourhood.
"le piéton" is a person walking on foot. "le trottoir" is the pavement they walk on, and "la ville" is the town.
"le passage piéton" is the striped place where pedestrians cross the road, a crosswalk (UK: pedestrian crossing). "le pont" is a bridge.

questions.prompt: The French word for "one-way street" is… ___
questions.explanation: "le sens unique" is a one-way street, where cars may drive in one direction only; the full form is « une rue à sens unique ».

units.title: Say It Your Way
units.description: Write the idea in French — Everyday situations, and more than one wording is right.

questions.prompt: Say what you did yesterday (go to the market).
acceptableAnswers: Hier, je suis allé au marché.
Hier, je suis allée au marché.
Je suis allé au marché hier.
Je suis allée au marché hier.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Hier, je suis allé au marché." Aller takes être in the passé composé, so a woman writes allée, and "au" is à + le before marché.

acceptableAnswers: Comment s'est passé ton week-end ?
Tu as passé un bon week-end ?
Qu'as-tu fait ce week-end ?
questions.explanation: "Comment s'est passé ton week-end ?" literally means "How did your weekend go?". It uses "se passer" in the passé composé with "être", and "ton" because you ask a friend.

questions.prompt: Say you are going to travel next summer.
acceptableAnswers: Je vais voyager l'été prochain.
L'été prochain, je pars en voyage.
Je compte voyager l'été prochain.
questions.explanation: "Je vais voyager l'été prochain." uses the near future: "aller" in the present plus the infinitive "voyager", for a plan you have already made.

acceptableAnswers: C'est cassé.
Ça ne marche pas.
C'est en panne.
questions.explanation: "C'est cassé." means "It's broken". "Cassé" is the past participle of "casser" (to break), used here like an adjective after "c'est".

questions.prompt: Ask for a table for two.
acceptableAnswers: Une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît.
Avez-vous une table pour deux ?
Je voudrais une table pour deux personnes.
questions.explanation: "Une table pour deux, s'il vous plaît." is the usual short request in a restaurant. You use "s'il vous plaît" because you are speaking politely to staff.

acceptableAnswers: J'ai oublié mes clés.
J'ai oublié mes clés à la maison.
Mes clés, je les ai oubliées.
questions.explanation: "J'ai oublié mes clés." uses the passé composé of "oublier" with "avoir" for a finished action. Keys are plural, so you say "mes clés".

questions.prompt: Ask if the seat is taken.
acceptableAnswers: Cette place est-elle libre ?
Est-ce que cette place est prise ?
La place est libre ?
questions.explanation: "Cette place est-elle libre ?" means "Is this seat free?". French asks either whether a seat is "libre" (free) or "prise" (taken), and here the subject is inverted to form a more formal question.

questions.prompt: Say you used to live in Lyon.
acceptableAnswers: J'habitais à Lyon avant.
Avant, j'habitais à Lyon.
Avant, je vivais à Lyon.
questions.explanation: "J'habitais à Lyon avant." uses the imparfait "habitais" to describe an ongoing past situation, which matches English "used to live".

questions.prompt: Recommend a restaurant to a friend.
acceptableAnswers: Je te recommande ce restaurant.
Ce restaurant est vraiment bon, essaie-le.
Tu devrais essayer ce restaurant.
questions.explanation: "Je te recommande ce restaurant." uses "te" because you are talking to a friend, and "recommander" means "to recommend".

questions.prompt: Ask someone what they think of a movie.
acceptableAnswers: Qu'est-ce que tu penses du film ?
Tu as aimé le film ?
Comment as-tu trouvé le film ?
questions.explanation: "Qu'est-ce que tu penses du film ?" uses "penser de" (to think of). "De" plus "le" becomes "du" before "film".

questions.prompt: Say you need to see a doctor.
acceptableAnswers: Je dois voir un médecin.
J'ai besoin de consulter un médecin.
Il faut que je voie un médecin.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Je dois voir un médecin." Everyday situations, and more than one wording is right.

questions.prompt: Explain that you missed the bus.
acceptableAnswers: J'ai raté le bus.
Le bus est parti sans moi.
J'ai manqué le bus.
questions.explanation: "J'ai raté le bus." uses the passé composé of "rater", the everyday verb for missing a bus or train ("manquer" is a little more formal).

questions.prompt: Ask how to get to the museum.
acceptableAnswers: Comment va-t-on au musée ?
Pour aller au musée, s'il vous plaît ?
Quel chemin faut-il prendre pour le musée ?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Comment va-t-on au musée ?" Everyday situations, and more than one wording is right.

questions.prompt: Say you are looking for a job.
acceptableAnswers: Je cherche un emploi.
Je suis à la recherche d'un travail.
Je cherche du travail.
questions.explanation: "Je cherche un emploi." uses "chercher" without a preposition: it already means "to look for", so never say "chercher pour".

questions.prompt: Ask a colleague for help with a task.
acceptableAnswers: Peux-tu m'aider avec ça ?
Pourriez-vous m'aider avec cette tâche ?
J'aurais besoin d'un coup de main.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Peux-tu m'aider avec ça ?" Everyday situations, and more than one wording is right.

questions.prompt: Say the weather was terrible yesterday.
acceptableAnswers: Il a fait un temps horrible hier.
Hier, le temps était affreux.
Le temps était vraiment mauvais hier.
questions.explanation: "Il a fait un temps horrible hier." uses the weather expression "il fait" in the passé composé, because yesterday's weather is a finished period.

acceptableAnswers: Et si on allait à la plage ?
On pourrait aller à la plage.
Allons à la plage !
questions.explanation: "Et si on allait à la plage ?" uses si + the imperfect to make a friendly suggestion. "On pourrait aller à la plage." or "Allons à la plage !" also work.

acceptableAnswers: J'ai déjà mangé.
J'ai déjà pris mon repas.
J'ai mangé, merci.
questions.explanation: "J'ai déjà mangé." uses the passé composé with "déjà" placed between the auxiliary and the past participle to say you have already eaten.

questions.prompt: Ask if there is a discount.
acceptableAnswers: Y a-t-il une réduction ?
Est-ce qu'il y a une remise ?
Faites-vous des réductions ?
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Y a-t-il une réduction ?" Everyday situations, and more than one wording is right.

questions.prompt: Say you will call back later.
acceptableAnswers: Je rappellerai plus tard.
Je vous rappelle plus tard.
Je te rappelle tout à l'heure.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Je rappellerai plus tard." Everyday situations, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Désolé pour le retard.
Désolée pour le retard.
Je suis en retard, toutes mes excuses.
questions.explanation: "Désolé pour le retard." is the everyday way to apologize for being late; a woman writes "Désolée" with an extra -e.

questions.prompt: Say you have never been to Italy.
acceptableAnswers: Je ne suis jamais allé en Italie.
Je ne suis jamais allée en Italie.
Je n'ai encore jamais visité l'Italie.
questions.explanation: One way to say it: "Je ne suis jamais allé en Italie." Everyday situations, and more than one wording is right.

acceptableAnswers: Quel est le mot de passe wifi ?
Avez-vous le mot de passe du wifi ?
Le wifi, c'est quoi le mot de passe ?
questions.explanation: "Quel est le mot de passe wifi ?" uses "quel" to ask which specific thing, here the wifi password; "Avez-vous le mot de passe du wifi ?" is a polite alternative.

questions.prompt: Say you plan to study tonight.
acceptableAnswers: Je vais étudier ce soir.

units.title: Speaking: Asking and Arranging
units.description: Say it out loud — Everyday phrases for asking, arranging and explaining.

questions.answer: Est-ce que tu es libre ce soir ?
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Est-ce que tu es libre ce soir ?" Starting with "Est-ce que" turns a statement into a yes/no question, and "tu" fits asking a friend.
Target phrase: "On peut se voir demain ?" In everyday speech "on" means "we", and a rising voice alone makes it a question.
Target phrase: "Je dois partir maintenant." "Devoir" plus an infinitive means "to have to", and the final "s" of "dois" and "t" of "maintenant" are silent.
Target phrase: "Pouvez-vous m'aider, s'il vous plaît ?" Inverting "vous pouvez" to "Pouvez-vous" gives a polite question for asking a stranger for help.
Target phrase: "Je cherche la gare." "Chercher" means "to look for" and takes no preposition, so there is no word for "for" before "la gare".
Target phrase: "C'est à quelle distance ?" This is a natural spoken way to ask how far away something is, with "à" before "quelle distance".
Target phrase: "Combien ça coûte ?" This is the everyday way to ask a price, and the final "-te" of "coûte" is pronounced.
Target phrase: "Je voudrais réserver une table." "Je voudrais" (I would like) is the polite form to use when booking at a restaurant.
Target phrase: "Avez-vous une chambre libre ?" Inverting to "Avez-vous" makes a polite question for a hotel receptionist, and "libre" means available.

questions.answer: Le train part à quelle heure ?
questions.explanation: Target phrase: "Le train part à quelle heure ?" In spoken French "à quelle heure" can come at the end of the question, with the voice rising.

questions.answer: J'étudie le français depuis deux ans.
questions.explanation: "J'étudie le français depuis deux ans." means "I've been studying French for two years." French uses the present tense with "depuis" for something still going on, and "deux ans" is linked with a "z" sound.
"Nous habitons ici depuis longtemps." means "We have lived here for a long time." The present tense goes with "depuis", and "nous habitons" is linked with a "z" sound.
"Elle arrive dans dix minutes." means "She's arriving in ten minutes." "Dans" plus a time means "in ... from now", and "dix" before "minutes" is said "dee".
"Il est parti hier soir." means "He left last night." "Partir" takes "être" in the past tense, so you say "est parti", and the final "t" of "parti" is not pronounced.

questions.answer: Je vais chez le médecin demain.
questions.explanation: "Je vais chez le médecin demain." means "I'm going to the doctor's tomorrow." Use "chez" when you go to a person's place, such as a doctor or a friend.
"Tu peux venir avec nous ?" means "Can you come with us?" A rising voice at the end turns the sentence into a question, and "tu" suits a friend.
"C'est une bonne idée." means "That's a good idea." "Idée" is feminine, so it takes "une" and "bonne".
"Je suis d'accord avec toi." means "I agree with you." French uses "être d'accord" (to be in agreement), and "toi" is the form used after "avec".
"Je ne suis pas d'accord." means "I don't agree." The negation "ne ... pas" goes around the verb "suis".

"Elle" is third person singular, so voir takes the -t ending: "voit".

units.title: Sentences: Reading
units.description: Present tense in short sentences — Choose the verb form that matches the subject.

questions.explanation: "Ils" is third person plural, so lire takes -ent: "lisent"; "lit" would be singular.
With "Je" the present of lire ends in -s: "lis".
With "Tu" lire takes -s, giving "lis" (the same spelling as the je form).
The subject "Vous" takes the -ez ending, so lire becomes "lisez".
"Elles" is third person plural, so lire takes -ent: "lisent".
"Elle" is third person singular, so lire takes -t: "lit".
The subject "Nous" takes the -ons ending, so lire becomes "lisons".
"Il" is third person singular, so lire takes -t: "lit".
The subject "Il" is third person singular, so lire takes the ending -t: "lit". "lisent" is for ils/elles and "lisez" for vous.
With "Je" the verb lire takes the ending -s: "lis". The other forms belong to vous, ils/elles and il/elle.
"Ils" is third person plural, so lire takes -ent: "lisent". "lisons" is for nous and "lit" for il.
"Elles" is third person plural, so lire takes -ent: "lisent". "lit" is singular and "lisons" goes with nous.
With "Tu" the verb lire takes the ending -s: "lis". "lit" is for il/elle and "lisez" for vous.
"Vous" takes the ending -ez: "lisez". "lisent" goes with ils/elles and "lit" with il/elle.
"Nous" takes the ending -ons: "lisons". "lisez" is for vous and "lisent" for ils/elles.

units.title: Passé Composé
units.description: Talking about the past — Passé composé with both avoir and être auxiliaries.

questions.explanation: Manger takes avoir, and with "J'" the form is "ai mangé". With avoir the participle does not agree with the subject, and the object "une pizza" comes after the verb, so there is no -e.
Regarder uses avoir, and "Tu" goes with "as", then the past participle in -é: "as regardé". An infinitive such as "regarder" cannot follow the auxiliary.
Parler takes avoir, and "Il" goes with "a" plus the participle: "a parlé". "Est parlé" uses the wrong auxiliary and "as" does not match il.
Finir takes avoir, and "Nous" goes with "avons" plus the participle "fini", which does not agree with the subject: "avons fini". "Avons finis" wrongly adds an -s.
Choisir takes avoir, and "Vous" goes with "avez" plus "choisi": "avez choisi". The participle does not agree because the object "le menu" comes after the verb, and "ont" belongs to ils.
"ont vendu" is right because "vendre" takes avoir, and "elles" needs "ont". The participle stays invariable since the object "leur maison" comes after the verb.
"suis allé" is right because "aller" takes être, and Paul is a man speaking, so the participle is masculine singular with no added -e or -s.

questions.prompt: Marc, tu ___ (venir) chez moi hier soir.
questions.explanation: "es venu" is right because "venir" takes être, and "tu" needs "es". Marc is a man, so the participle is masculine singular, with no -e or -s.
"est parti" is right because "partir" takes être, and "il" is masculine singular, so the participle gets no -e or -s.

questions.prompt: Paul et moi, nous ___ (arriver) en retard.
questions.explanation: "sommes arrivés" is right because "arriver" takes être. "Paul et moi" means "nous", a mixed or masculine group, so the participle is masculine plural with -s.
"est née" is right because "naître" takes être, and "elle" is feminine singular, so the participle takes an extra -e.
"sont restés" is right because "rester" takes être, and "ils" is masculine plural, so the participle takes -s.
"ai eu" is right because "avoir" forms its own passé composé with avoir, and "j'" needs "ai". The object "une bonne idée" follows the verb, so "eu" does not agree.
"as été" is right because "être" takes avoir in the passé composé, and "tu" goes with "as".
"a fait" is right because "faire" takes avoir, and "il" needs "a". The object "ses devoirs" comes after the verb, so "fait" stays invariable.
"avons vu" is right because "voir" takes avoir, and "nous" needs "avons". The object "un bon film" follows the verb, so "vu" does not agree.
"avez pris" is right because "prendre" takes avoir, "vous" needs "avez", and the irregular participle is "pris", not "prendu".
"ont dit" is right because dire takes avoir, and the past participle "dit" does not agree here since there is no preceding direct object.
"ai écrit" is right because j' needs the avoir form "ai", and écrire has the irregular participle "écrit", with no agreement since "une lettre" comes after the verb.
"as lu" is right because tu goes with "as" and lire has the irregular participle "lu", not "lit".
"a bu" is right because boire forms its passé composé with avoir and has the irregular participle "bu", not "boit" or "buvé".
"avons compris" is right because nous takes "avons" and comprendre has the participle "compris", with no feminine -e since "la leçon" follows the verb.
"avez mis" is right because mettre takes avoir and has the irregular participle "mis", with no agreement since "la table" comes after the verb.
Used without a direct object, descendre takes être, and the participle agrees with the feminine plural subject elles, giving "sont descendues".
questions.meaning: they went down, they came down
questions.example: Elles sont descendues à la gare.

questions.explanation: "ai perdu" is right because perdre takes avoir (j' + "ai") and the participle "perdu" does not agree, since "mes clés" comes after the verb.

units.title: Adjectives & Descriptions
units.description: Describing people and things — Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).

questions.explanation: "content" means happy in the sense of pleased or satisfied, and this is its masculine form.
sad (feeling) → triste. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
"grand" means tall when describing a person (and big for a thing), and this is its masculine form.

questions.prompt: The French word for "short" (not tall) is…
questions.explanation: "petit" describes a person or thing that is short in height (or small); for short in length, French uses "court" instead.
"belle" is the feminine form of "beau" (beautiful); it is used with feminine nouns, as in une belle maison.
ugly → laid. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
young → jeune. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
"vieux" means "old"; it is the masculine form, and it becomes "vieille" in the feminine.
"fort" means "strong"; it is the masculine form, and it becomes "forte" in the feminine.
weak → faible. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
intelligent → intelligent. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
funny → drôle. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
serious → sérieux. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
kind (feminine) → "gentille": the feminine of "gentil" doubles the l and adds -e.
generous → généreux. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
"timide" means shy; it ends in -e, so it stays the same for masculine and feminine (un garçon timide, une fille timide).
brave → courageux. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
"paresseux" means "lazy"; it is the masculine form, and it becomes "paresseuse" in the feminine.
hardworking → travailleur. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
rich → riche. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
poor → pauvre. Common descriptive adjectives (masculine form).
"facile" means easy; it ends in -e, so it stays the same for masculine and feminine (un test facile, une question facile).
"difficile" means "difficult"; it already ends in -e, so it keeps the same form for masculine and feminine.
"intéressant" means "interesting"; it is the masculine form, and it becomes "intéressante" in the feminine.
"ennuyeux" means "boring"; it is the masculine form, and it becomes "ennuyeuse" in the feminine.

units.title: Travel Phrases
units.description: Getting around abroad in French — Everyday travel vocabulary for airports, trains, and hotels.

questions.prompt: Je voudrais ___ un billet, s'il vous plaît.
questions.explanation: After "Je voudrais" French needs an infinitive, so "réserver" (to book) fits with "un billet"; the other options are conjugated or participle forms.
"salle d'attente" is the fixed phrase for a waiting room, and after "d'" you need the noun "attente", not a verb or adjective.
questions.example: Où est la salle d'attente ?

questions.prompt: Le vol est ___ de deux heures.
questions.explanation: "retardé" means delayed, which fits "de deux heures" (by two hours); a flight cannot be cancelled, booked or full by two hours.
The clue "(passport)" points to "passeport", a masculine noun that fits "mon"; "valise" is a suitcase and "annulé" means cancelled.

questions.prompt: Avez-vous encore une chambre ___ pour ce soir ?
questions.explanation: "libre" is right: "chambre" is singular feminine, so "libre" (which has one form for both genders) agrees, and a hotel asks for a free room; "libres" is plural, while "occupée" and "pleine" would not make sense when asking for a vacancy.
questions.example: Avez-vous une chambre libre pour ce soir ?

questions.explanation: You ask the price of a ticket to a destination, so "billet" fits. A "quai" is a platform, a "guichet" a ticket window and a "retard" a delay, none of which has a price.

questions.prompt: Le train part du ___ numéro trois.
questions.explanation: A train departs from a numbered platform, and "quai" means platform. A "guichet" is a ticket window, a "billet" is a ticket and a "vol" is a flight.

questions.prompt: J'ai besoin d'un ___ pour recharger mon téléphone.
questions.explanation: To charge a phone abroad you need a plug adapter, which is "adaptateur" in French. A ticket, a ticket window or a taxi cannot recharge a phone.

questions.prompt: La ___ est-elle incluse dans le prix ?
questions.explanation: You ask whether the tax is included in the price, and "taxe" is the feminine noun that fits after "La". "Monnaie" is change, "douane" is customs and "sortie" is an exit, so none of them can be included in a price.
You can call a vehicle to come and pick you up, so "taxi" fits "appeler un ___". A ticket, a platform or a ticket window cannot be called.

questions.prompt: Nous devons ___ dans vingt minutes, porte 12.
questions.explanation: After "Nous devons" the next verb stays in the infinitive, so "embarquer" is right. "Embarquons" and "embarquez" are conjugated forms, and "embarqué" is a participle.
questions.meaning: to board (a plane, ship or train)
questions.example: Nous devons embarquer avant dix heures.

questions.prompt: Le ___ a trente minutes de retard.
questions.explanation: The article "Le" needs a masculine noun, and "bus" is the masculine vehicle that can run thirty minutes late. "Navette", "gare" and "voiture" are feminine, so "le" does not fit them.

questions.prompt: J'ai oublié ma carte d'___. (ID card)
questions.explanation: The clue "(ID card)" points to "identité": a carte d'identité is an ID card, while a carte d'embarquement is a boarding pass and a carte d'abonnement is a season ticket.
"Faire de la monnaie" means to get small change, and "de la" needs a feminine singular noun such as "monnaie". "Argent" and "chèque" are masculine and "billets" is plural, so they do not fit "de la".
questions.example: Avez-vous de la monnaie pour le bus ?

questions.explanation: "dépôt" is correct here. Everyday travel vocabulary for airports, trains, and hotels.
The article "la" needs a feminine noun, and "région" is the only feminine option, as well as something a map can show. "Quartier", "pays" and "aéroport" are all masculine.
"fenêtre" is correct here. Everyday travel vocabulary for airports, trains, and hotels.

questions.prompt: Le personnel de bord nous a donné des ___.
questions.explanation: The article "des" needs a plural noun, which rules out the singular "consigne", "conseil" and "information". Cabin crew give passengers "instructions" (safety directions).

questions.prompt: Notre premier vol avait du retard, alors nous avons raté notre ___.
questions.explanation: "notre" is singular, so the plural options (vols, trains, billets) don't fit. You miss a "correspondance", meaning a connecting train or flight.
questions.meaning: connection, transfer between trains or flights

questions.explanation: "un" and "gratuit" are masculine, and "petit-déjeuner" is the only masculine noun here (boisson, navette and connexion are feminine). Hotels commonly include a free breakfast.
questions.example: L'hôtel propose un petit-déjeuner gratuit.

questions.prompt: Le ___ est à dix minutes à pied.
questions.explanation: "Le" is masculine, so the feminine nouns "gare", "plage" and "station" are ruled out. "centre-ville" is the masculine noun that fits.

questions.prompt: Avez-vous besoin d'un ___ pour ce pays ?
questions.explanation: "un" is masculine, which rules out the feminine options (autorisation, assurance, vaccination). A "visa" is the entry document you need for a country.

questions.prompt: Notre vol a été ___ à cause de la météo.
questions.explanation: In the passive "a été ___", the participle agrees with the subject "vol", which is masculine singular, so "annulé" with no added ending.
The clue "(luggage)" gives "bagages", the plural noun for bags and cases that a customs officer opens. "valise" is singular and doesn't fit "mes".

questions.prompt: Je cherche l'___ principale de l'aéroport.
questions.explanation: "l'" needs a singular noun starting with a vowel and "principale" is feminine, so "entrée" fits; "entrées" is plural and "accueil" is masculine. You look for the main entrance of an airport.

units.title: Futur Simple
units.description: Talking about the future — Futur simple conjugation of common verbs.

questions.explanation: The subject "je" in the futur simple takes the ending -ai added to the infinitive, giving "parlerai"; "demain" confirms the future.
The subject "tu" in the futur simple takes the ending -as added to the infinitive, giving "finiras"; "ce soir" points to the future.

questions.prompt: Il ___ (partir) en vacances la semaine prochaine.
questions.explanation: The subject "il" in the futur simple takes the ending -a added to the infinitive, giving "partira"; "la semaine prochaine" confirms the future.
The subject "nous" in the futur simple takes -ons added to the infinitive, giving "voyagerons"; "l'année prochaine" confirms the future.
The subject "Vous" takes the futur simple ending -ez, so the infinitive arriver + -ez gives "arriverez".
"Elles" is third-person plural, so venir takes the irregular future stem viendr- plus -ont: "viendront".
Être has the irregular future stem ser-, and "Je" takes the ending -ai, giving "serai".
Avoir has the irregular future stem aur-, and "Tu" takes the ending -as, giving "auras".
Faire has the irregular future stem fer-, and "Il" takes the ending -a, giving "fera".
questions.meaning: it will be (weather); he will do

questions.explanation: Aller has the irregular future stem ir-, and "Nous" takes the ending -ons, giving "irons"; "allerons" is not a French form.
Pouvoir has the irregular future stem pourr- (with double r), and "Vous" takes -ez, giving "pourrez".
Vouloir has the irregular future stem voudr-, and "Elles" (third-person plural) takes -ont, giving "voudront".
Savoir has the irregular future stem saur-, and "Je" takes the ending -ai, giving "saurai".
Voir has the irregular future stem verr- (double r), and "Tu" takes the ending -as, giving "verras".
Envoyer has the irregular future stem enverr-, and "Il" takes the ending -a, giving "enverra".
Devoir has the irregular future stem devr-, and "Nous" takes the ending -ons, giving "devrons".
The subject "Vous" takes the futur simple ending -ez, and recevoir has the future stem recevr-, giving "recevrez".
The subject "Elles" is third person plural, so the ending is -ont, and tenir has the irregular stem tiendr-, giving "tiendront".
Courir has the irregular future stem courr- (double r), and "Je" takes the ending -ai, giving "courrai".

questions.prompt: Tu ___ (mourir) de rire en voyant ça.
questions.explanation: Mourir has the irregular future stem mourr- (double r), and "Tu" takes the ending -as, giving "mourras".
Venir has the irregular future stem viendr-, and "Il" takes the ending -a, giving "viendra".
Finir is a regular verb: the infinitive finir plus the ending -ons for "Nous" gives "finirons".
Choisir is regular: the infinitive plus the ending -ez for "Vous" gives "choisirez".
Réussir is regular, and "Elles" (third person plural) takes the ending -ont, giving "réussiront".
questions.meaning: they will succeed, they will pass

questions.explanation: Acheter changes to the future stem achèter- (with è), and "Je" takes the ending -ai, giving "achèterai".
questions.example: J'achèterai une nouvelle voiture bientôt.

units.title: Imparfait
units.description: Describing the past — Imperfect tense for past habits and descriptions.

questions.prompt: Quand j'étais petit, je ___ (jouer) souvent dehors.
questions.explanation: "Quand j'étais petit" signals a repeated childhood habit, so the imparfait is used, and "je" takes the ending -ais: "jouais".
